senses.d: Every one of the two or more individuals composing a number of objects, considered separately from the rest. It is used either with or without a following noun; as, each of you or each one of you.
q: It is a bad thing that men should hate each other; but it is far worse that they should contract the habit of cutting one another's throats without hatred.
Let each His adamantine coat gird well.
In each cheek appears a pretty dimple.
Then draw we nearer day by day, Each to his brethren, all to God.
The oak and the elm have each a distinct character.

senses.d: Every; — sometimes used interchangeably with every.
q: I know each lane and every alley green.
In short each man's happiness depends upon himself.

Each.etym: [OE. eche, ælc, elk, ilk, AS. ælc; ā always + gelīc like; akin to OD. iegelik, OHG. ēogilīh, MHG. iegelīch, G. jeglich. √209. See 3d Aye, Like, and cf. Either, Every, Ilk.]

senses.d: Any large, rapacious bird of the Falcon family, esp. of the genera Aquila and Haliæetus. The eagle is remarkable for strength, size, graceful figure, keenness of vision, and extraordinary flight. The most noted species are the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaëtus); the imperial eagle of Europe (A. mogilnik or imperialis); the American bald eagle (Haliæetus leucocephalus); the European sea eagle (H. albicilla); and the great harpy eagle (Thrasaetus harpyia). The figure of the eagle, as the king of birds, is commonly used as an heraldic emblem, and also for standards and emblematic devices. See Bald eagle, Harpy, and Golden eagle.
A gold coin of the United States, of the value of ten dollars.
A northern constellation, containing Altair, a star of the first magnitude. See Aquila.
The figure of an eagle borne as an emblem on the standard of the ancient Romans, or so used upon the seal or standard of any people.
q: Though the Roman eagle shadow thee.

Eagle.etym: [OE. egle, F. aigle, fr. L. aquila; prob. named from its color, fr. aquilus dark-colored, brown; cf. Lith. aklas blind. Cf. Aquiline.]

senses.d: The organ of hearing; the external ear.
The sense of hearing; the perception of sounds; the power of discriminating between different tones; as, a nice ear for music; — in the singular only.
q: Songs . . . not all ungrateful to thine ear.

senses.d: That which resembles in shape or position the ear of an animal; any prominence or projection on an object, — usually one for support or attachment; a lug; a handle; as, the ears of a tub, a skillet, or dish. The ears of a boat are outside kneepieces near the bow. See Illust. of Bell.
Same as Acroterium.
Privilege of being kindly heard; favor; attention.
q: Dionysius . . . would give no ear to his suit.
Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.

Ear.etym: [AS. eáre; akin to OFries. áre, ár, OS. �ra, D. oor, OHG. �ra, G. ohr, Icel. eyra, Sw. öra, Dan. öre, Goth. auso, L. auris, Lith. ausis, Russ. ukho, Gr. �; cf. L. audire to hear, Gr. �, Skr. av to favor , protect. Cf. Auricle, Orillon.]

senses.d: To take in with the ears; to hear.
The spike or head of any cereal (as, wheat, rye, barley, Indian corn, etc.), containing the kernels.
q: First the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.

Ear.etym: [AS. ear; akin to D. aar, OHG. ahir, G. ähre, Icel., Sw., & Dan. ax, Goth. ahs. ���. Cf. Awn, Edge.]

senses.d: To put forth ears in growing; to form ears, as grain; as, this corn ears well.
To plow or till; to cultivate.

Ear.etym: [OE. erien, AS. erian; akin to OFries. era, OHG. erran, MHG. eren, ern, Prov. G. aren, ären, Icel. erja, Goth. arjan, Lith. arti, OSlav. orati, L. arare, Gr. �. Cf. Arable.]

senses.d: Having (such or so many) ears; — used in composition; as, long-eared-eared; sharp-eared; full-eared; ten-eared.
Having external ears; having tufts of feathers resembling ears.
A line used to fasten the upper corners of a sail to the yard or gaff; — also called head earing.
A line for hauling the reef cringle to the yard; — also called reef earing.
A line fastening the corners of an awning to the rigging or stanchions.
Coming into ear, as corn.
A plowing of land.
q: Neither earing nor harvest.

senses.d: Soon; in good season; seasonably; betimes; as, come early.
q: Those that me early shall find me.
You must wake and call me early.

Early.etym: [OE. erli, erliche, AS. ǣrlīce; ǣr sooner + līc like. See Ere, and Like.]

senses.d: In advance of the usual or appointed time; in good season; prior in time; among or near the first; — opposed to late; as, the early bird; an early spring; early fruit.
q: Early and provident fear is the mother of safety.
The doorsteps and threshold with the early grass springing up about them.

senses.d: Coming in the first part of a period of time, or among the first of successive acts, events, etc.
q: Seen in life's early morning sky.
The forms of its earlier manhood.
The earliest poem he composed was in his seventeenth summer.

senses.d: To merit or deserve, as by labor or service; to do that which entitles one to (a reward, whether the reward is received or not).
q: The high repute Which he through hazard huge must earn.

senses.d: To acquire by labor, service, or performance; to deserve and receive as compensation or wages; as, to earn a good living; to earn honors or laurels.
q: I earn that I eat.
The bread I have earned by the hazard of my life or the sweat of my brow.

Earn.etym: [AS. earnian; akin to OHG. arn�n to reap, aran harvest, G. ernte, Goth. asans harvest, asneis hireling, AS. esne; cf. Icel. önn working season, work.]

senses.d: To grieve.
To long; to yearn.
q: And ever as he rode, his heart did earn To prove his puissance in battle brave.

senses.d: To curdle, as milk.

Earn.etym: [AS. irnan to run. √11. See Rennet, and cf. Yearnings.]

senses.d: Seriousness; reality; fixed determination; eagerness; intentness.
q: Take heed that this jest do not one day turn to earnest.
And given in earnest what I begged in jest.

Earnest.etym: [AS. eornost, eornest; akin to OHG. ernust, G. ernst; cf. Icel. orrosta battle, perh. akin to Gr. � to excite, L. oriri to rise.]

senses.d: Ardent in the pursuit of an object; eager to obtain or do; zealous with sincerity; with hearty endeavor; heartfelt; fervent; hearty; — used in a good sense; as, earnest prayers.
q: An earnest advocate to plead for him.

senses.d: Intent; fixed closely; as, earnest attention.
Serious; important.
q: They whom earnest lets do often hinder.

Earnest.syn: Eager; warm; zealous; ardent; animated; importunate; fervent; sincere; serious; hearty; urgent. See Eager.

senses.d: To use in earnest.
q: To earnest them with men.

senses.d: Something given, or a part paid beforehand, as a pledge; pledge; handsel; a token of what is to come.
q: Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.
And from his coffers Received the golden earnest of our death.

senses.d: Something of value given by the buyer to the seller, by way of token or pledge, to bind the bargain and prove the sale.

Earnest.etym: [Prob. corrupted fr. F. arrhes, L. arra, arrha, arrhabo, Gr. αρραβὤν, of Semitic origin, cf. Heb. ērāvōn; or perh. fr. W. ernes, akin to Gael. earlas, perh. fr. L. arra. Cf. Arles, Earles penny.]

senses.d: In an earnest manner.
An ornament consisting of a ring passed through the lobe of the ear, with or without a pendant.
The globe or planet which we inhabit; the world, in distinction from the sun, moon, or stars. Also, this world as the dwelling place of mortals, in distinction from the dwelling place of spirits.
q: That law preserves the earth a sphere And guides the planets in their course.
In heaven, or earth, or under earth, in hell.

senses.d: The solid materials which make up the globe, in distinction from the air or water; the dry land.
q: God called the dry land earth.
He is pure air and fire, and the dull elements of earth and water never appear in him.

senses.d: The softer inorganic matter composing part of the surface of the globe, in distinction from the firm rock; soil of all kinds, including gravel, clay, loam, and the like; sometimes, soil favorable to the growth of plants; the visible surface of the globe; the ground; as, loose earth; rich earth.
q: Give him a little earth for charity.

senses.d: A part of this globe; a region; a country; land.
q: Would I had never trod this English earth.

senses.d: Worldly things, as opposed to spiritual things; the pursuits, interests, and allurements of this life.
q: Our weary souls by earth beguiled.

senses.d: The people on the globe.
q: The whole earth was of one language.

senses.d: Any earthy-looking metallic oxide, as alumina, glucina, zirconia, yttria, and thoria.
A hole in the ground, where an animal hides himself; as, the earth of a fox.
q: They course the poor conies out of their earths.

Earth.etym: [AS. eor�e; akin to OS. ertha, OFries. irthe, D. aarde, OHG. erda, G. erde, Icel. jör�, Sw. & Dan. jord, Goth. aīrpa, OHG. ero, Gr. �, adv., to earth, and perh. to E. ear to plow.]

senses.d: To hide, or cause to hide, in the earth; to chase into a burrow or den.
To cover with earth or mold; to inter; to bury; — sometimes with up.
q: The miser earths his treasure, and the thief, Watching the mole, half beggars him ere noon.
Why this in earthing up a carcass?

senses.d: To burrow.
A plowing.
q: Such land as ye break up for barley to sow, Two earths at the least, ere ye sow it, bestow.

senses.d: The connection of any part an electric conductor with the ground; specif., the connection of a telegraph line with the ground through a fault or otherwise.
Made of earth; made of burnt or baked clay, or other like substances; as, an earthen vessel or pipe.
Pertaining to the earth; belonging to this world, or to man's existence on the earth; not heavenly or spiritual; carnal; worldly; as, earthly joys; earthly flowers; earthly praise.
q: This earthly load Of death, called life.
Whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.

senses.d: Of all things on earth; possible; conceivable.
q: What earthly benefit can be the result?

senses.d: Made of earth; earthy.

Earthly.syn: Gross; material; sordid; mean; base; vile; low; unsubstantial; temporary; corrupt; groveling.

senses.d: In the manner of the earth or its people; worldly.
q: Took counsel from his guiding eyes To make this wisdom earthly wise.

senses.d: A shaking, trembling, or concussion of the earth, due to subterranean causes, often accompanied by a rumbling noise. The wave of shock sometimes traverses half a hemisphere, destroying cities and many thousand lives; — called also earthdin, earthquave, and earthshock.
Like, or characteristic of, an earthquake; loud; startling.
q: The earthquake voice of victory.

senses.d: Consisting of, or resembling, earth; terrene; earthlike; as, earthy matter.
q: How pale she looks, And of an earthy cold!
All over earthy, like a piece of earth.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the earth or to, this world; earthly; terrestrial; carnal.
q: The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is from heaven. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy.
Earthy spirits black and envious are.

senses.d: Gross; low; unrefined.
Without luster, or dull and roughish to the touch; as, an earthy fracture.
Satisfaction; pleasure; hence, accommodation; entertainment.
q: They him besought Of harbor and or ease as for hire penny.

senses.d: Freedom from anything that pains or troubles; as: (a) Relief from labor or effort; rest; quiet; relaxation; as, ease of body.
q: Usefulness comes by labor, wit by ease.
Give yourself ease from the fatigue of watching.

senses.d: Freedom from care, solicitude, or anything that annoys or disquiets; tranquillity; peace; comfort; security; as, ease of mind.
q: Among these nations shalt thou find no ease.
Take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.

senses.d: Freedom from constraint, formality, difficulty, embarrassment, etc.; facility; liberty; naturalness; — said of manner, style, etc.; as, ease of style, of behavior, of address.
q: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance.
Whate'er he did was done with so much ease, In him alone 't was natural to please.

Ease.syn: Rest; quiet; repose; comfortableness; tranquillity; facility; easiness; readiness.
Ease.etym: [OE. ese, eise, F. aise; akin to Pr. ais, aise, OIt. asio, It. agio; of uncertain origin; cf. L. ansa handle, occasion, opportunity. Cf. Agio, Disease.]

senses.d: To free from anything that pains, disquiets, or oppresses; to relieve from toil or care; to give rest, repose, or tranquillity to; — often with of; as, to ease of pain; to ease the body or mind.
q: Eased the putting off These troublesome disguises which we wear.
Sing, and I 'll ease thy shoulders of thy load.

senses.d: To render less painful or oppressive; to mitigate; to alleviate.
q: My couch shall ease my complaint.

senses.d: To release from pressure or restraint; to move gently; to lift slightly; to shift a little; as, to ease a bar or nut in machinery.
To entertain; to furnish with accommodations.

Ease.syn: To relieve; disburden; quiet; calm; tranquilize; assuage; alleviate; allay; mitigate; appease; pacify.
Ease.etym: [OE. esen, eisen, OF. aisier. See Ease, n.]

senses.d: With ease; without difficulty or much effort; as, this task may be easily performed; that event might have been easily foreseen.
Without pain, anxiety, or disturbance; as, to pass life well and easily.
Readily; without reluctance; willingly.
q: Not soon provoked, she easily forgives.

senses.d: Smoothly; quietly; gently; gracefully; without �umult or discord.
Without shaking or jolting; commodiously; as, a carriage moves easily.

The point in the heavens where the sun is seen to rise at the equinox, or the corresponding point on the earth; that one of the four cardinal points of the compass which is in a direction at right angles to that of north and south, and which is toward the right hand of one who faces the north; the point directly opposite to the west.
q: The east began kindle.

senses.d: The eastern parts of the earth; the regions or countries which lie east of Europe; the orient. In this indefinite sense, the word is applied to Asia Minor, Syria, Chaldea, Persia, India, China, etc.; as, the riches of the East; the diamonds and pearls of the East; the kings of the East.
q: The gorgeous East, with richest hand, Showers on her kings barbaric pearl and gold.

senses.d: Formerly, the part of the United States east of the Alleghany Mountains, esp. the Eastern, or New England, States; now, commonly, the whole region east of the Mississippi River, esp. that which is north of Maryland and the Ohio River; — usually with the definite article; as, the commerce of the East is not independent of the agriculture of the West.

East.etym: [OE. est, east, AS. eást; akin to D. oost, oosten, OHG. ōstan, G. ost, osten, Icel. austr, Sw. ost, Dan. öst, östen, Lith. auszra dawn, L. aurora (for ausosa), Gr. ηὤσ, ἕοσ, ἄυωσ, Skr. ushas; cf. Skr. ush to burn, L. urere. √149, 288. Cf. Aurora, Easter, Sterling.]

senses.d: Toward the rising sun; or toward the point where the sun rises when in the equinoctial; as, the east gate; the east border; the east side; the east wind is a wind that blows from the east.
Eastward.
To move toward the east; to veer from the north or south toward the east; to orientate.
Designating, or situated in, that part of a church which contains the choir or chancel; as, the east front of a cathedral.

An annual church festival commemorating Christ's resurrection, and occurring on Sunday, the second day after Good Friday. It corresponds to the pascha or passover of the Jews, and most nations still give it this name under the various forms of pascha, pasque, pâque, or pask.
The day on which the festival is observed; Easter day.
q: Sundays by thee more glorious break, An Easter day in every week.

Easter.etym: [AS. eáster, eástran, paschal feast, Easter; akin to G. ostern; fr. AS. Eástre, a goddess of light or spring, in honor of whom a festival was celebrated in April; whence this month was called in AS. Eástermōnað. From the root of E. east. See East.]

senses.d: To veer to the east; — said of the wind.
Toward the east; in the direction of east from some point or place; as, New Haven lies eastward from New York.
At ease; free from pain, trouble, or constraint
Not causing, or attended with, pain or disquiet, or much exertion; affording ease or rest; as, an easy carriage; a ship having an easy motion; easy movements, as in dancing.
Not difficult; requiring little labor or effort; slight; inconsiderable; as, an easy task; an easy victory.
q: It were an easy leap.

senses.d: Causing ease; giving freedom from care or labor; furnishing comfort; commodious; as, easy circumstances; an easy chair or cushion.
Not making resistance or showing unwillingness; tractable; yielding; complying; ready.
q: He gained their easy hearts.
He is too tyrannical to be an easy monarch.

senses.d: Moderate; sparing; frugal.
Not straitened as to money matters; as, the market is easy; — opposed to tight.

Easy.syn: Quiet; comfortable; manageable; tranquil; calm; facile; unconcerned.
Easy.etym: [OF. aisié, F. aisé, prop. p. p. of OF. aisier. See Ease, v. t.]

senses.d: To chew and swallow as food; to devour; — said especially of food not liquid; as, to eat bread.
q: They . . . ate the sacrifices of the dead.
The lean . . . did eat up the first seven fat kine.
The lion had not eaten the carcass.
With stories told of many a feat, How fairy Mab the junkets eat.
The island princes overbold Have eat our substance.
His wretched estate is eaten up with mortgages.

senses.d: To corrode, as metal, by rust; to consume the flesh, as a cancer; to waste or wear away; to destroy gradually; to cause to disappear.

Eat.etym: [OE. eten, AS. etan; akin to OS. etan, OFries. eta, D. eten, OHG. ezzan, G. essen, Icel. eta, Sw. äta, Dan. æde, Goth. itan, Ir. & Gael. ith, W. ysu, L. edere, Gr. ἔδειν, Skr. ad. √6. Cf. Etch, Fret to rub, Edible.]

senses.d: To take food; to feed; especially, to take solid, in distinction from liquid, food; to board.
q: He did eat continually at the king's table.

senses.d: To taste or relish; as, it eats like tender beef.
To make one's way slowly.
One who, or that which, eats.
The act of tasking food; the act of consuming or corroding.
Something fit to be eaten; food; as, a peach is good eating.
A hard, heavy, and durable wood, which admits of a fine polish or gloss. The usual color is black, but it also occurs red or green.

Ebony.etym: [F. ébène, L. ebenus, fr. Gr. �; prob. of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. hobnīm, pl. Cf. Ebon.]

senses.d: Made of ebony, or resembling ebony; black; as, an ebony countenance.
q: This ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into smiling.

senses.d: The garden where Adam and Eve first dwelt; hence, a delightful region or residence.

Eden.etym: [Heb. ēden delight, pleasure; also, a place of pleasure, Eden.]

senses.d: The thin cutting side of the blade of an instrument; as, the edge of an ax, knife, sword, or scythe. Hence, figuratively, that which cuts as an edge does, or wounds deeply, etc.
q: He which hath the sharp sword with two edges.
Slander, Whose edge is sharper than the sword.

senses.d: Any sharp terminating border; a margin; a brink; extreme verge; as, the edge of a table, a precipice.
q: Upon the edge of yonder coppice.
In worst extremes, and on the perilous edge Of battle.
Pursue even to the very edge of destruction.

senses.d: Sharpness; readiness or fitness to cut; keenness; intenseness of desire.
q: The full edge of our indignation.
Death and persecution lose all the ill that they can have, if we do not set an edge upon them by our fears and by our vices.

senses.d: The border or part adjacent to the line of division; the beginning or early part; as, in the edge of evening.

Edge.etym: [OE. eg, egge, AS. ecg; akin to OHG. ekka, G. ecke, Icel. & Sw. egg, Dan. eg, and to L. acies, Gr. ακἤ point, Skr. açri edge. √1. Cf. Egg, v. t., Eager, Ear spike of corn, Acute.]

senses.d: To furnish with an edge as a tool or weapon; to sharpen.
q: To edge her champion's sword.

senses.d: To shape or dress the edge of, as with a tool.
To furnish with a fringe or border; as, to edge a dress; to edge a garden with box.
q: Hills whose tops were edged with groves.

senses.d: To make sharp or keen, figuratively; to incite; to exasperate; to goad; to urge or egg on.
q: By such reasonings, the simple were blinded, and the malicious edged.

senses.d: To move little by little or cautiously, as by pressing forward edgewise; as, edging their chairs forwards.
To move sideways; to move gradually; as, edge along this way.
To sail close to the wind.
q: I must edge up on a point of wind.

senses.d: The act of edifying, or the state of being edified; a building up, especially in a moral or spiritual sense; moral, intellectual, or spiritual improvement; instruction.
q: The assured edification of his church.
Out of these magazines I shall supply the town with what may tend to their edification.

senses.d: A building or edifice.

Edification.etym: [L. aedificatio: cf. F. édification. See Edify.]

senses.d: To build; to construct.
q: There was a holy chapel edified.

senses.d: To instruct and improve, especially in moral and religious knowledge; to teach.
q: It does not appear probable that our dispute would either edify or enlighten the public.

senses.d: To teach or persuade.

Edify.etym: [F. édifier, L. aedificare; aedes a building, house, orig., a fireplace (akin to Gr. � to burn, Skr. idh to kindle, OHG. eit funeral pile, AS. ād, OIr. aed fire) + facere to make. See Fact, -fy.]

senses.d: To improve.
Instructing; improving; as, an edifying conversation.
One of the descendants of Esau or Edom, the brother of Jacob; an Idumean.
Execution; performance; realization; operation; as, the law goes into effect in May.
q: That no compunctious visitings of nature Shake my fell purpose, nor keep peace between The effect and it.

senses.d: Manifestation; expression; sign.
q: All the large effects That troop with majesty.

senses.d: In general: That which is produced by an agent or cause; the event which follows immediately from an antecedent, called the cause; result; consequence; outcome; fruit; as, the effect of luxury.
q: The effect is the unfailing index of the amount of the cause.

senses.d: Impression left on the mind; sensation produced.
q: Patchwork . . . introduced for oratorical effect.
The effect was heightened by the wild and lonely nature of the place.

senses.d: Power to produce results; efficiency; force; importance; account; as, to speak with effect.
Consequence intended; purpose; meaning; general intent; — with to.
q: They spake to her to that effect.

senses.d: The purport; the sum and substance.
Reality; actual meaning; fact, as distinguished from mere appearance.
q: No other in effect than what it seems.

senses.d: Goods; movables; personal estate; — sometimes used to embrace real as well as personal property; as, the people escaped from the town with their effects.
q: Resolving all events, with their effects And manifold results, into the will And arbitration wise of the Supreme.
Shun the bitter consequence, for know, The day thou eatest thereof, . . . thou shalt die.

Effect.etym: [L. effectus, fr. efficere, effectum, to effect; ex + facere to make: cf. F. effet, formerly also spelled effect. See Fact.]

senses.d: To produce, as a cause or agent; to cause to be.
q: So great a body such exploits to effect.

senses.d: To bring to pass; to execute; to enforce; to achieve; to accomplish.
q: To effect that which the divine counsels had decreed.
They sailed away without effecting their purpose.

Effect.syn: To accomplish; fulfill; achieve; complete; execute; perform; attain. See Accomplish.

senses.d: Producing, or having adequate power or force to produce, an intended effect; adequate; efficient; operative; decisive.
q: Effectual steps for the suppression of the rebellion.

senses.d: With effect; efficaciously.
Actually; in effect.
Having some characteristic of a woman, as delicacy, luxuriousness, etc.; soft or delicate to an unmanly degree; womanish; weak.
q: The king, by his voluptuous life and mean marriage, became effeminate, and less sensible of honor.
An effeminate and unmanly foppery.

senses.d: Womanlike; womanly; tender; — in a good sense.
q: Gentle, kind, effeminate remorse.

Effeminate.etym: [L. effeminatus, p. p. of effeminare to make a woman of; ex out + femina a woman. See Feminine, a.]

senses.d: To make womanish; to make soft and delicate; to weaken.
q: It will not corrupt or effeminate children's minds.

senses.d: To grow womanish or weak.
q: In a slothful peace both courage will effeminate and manners corrupt.

senses.d: The oval or roundish body laid by domestic poultry and other birds, tortoises, etc. It consists of a yolk, usually surrounded by the “white” or albumen, and inclosed in a shell or strong membrane.
A simple cell, from the development of which the young of animals are formed; ovum; germ cell.
Anything resembling an egg in form.

Egg.etym: [OE., fr. Icel. egg; akin to AS. æg (whence OE. ey), Sw. ägg, Dan. æg, G. & D. ei, and prob. to OSlav. aje, jaje, L. ovum, Gr. ᾠόν, Ir. ugh, Gael. ubh, and perh. to L. avis bird. Cf. Oval.]

senses.d: To urge on; to instigate; to incite�
q: Adam and Eve he egged to ill.
did egg him on to tell How fair she was.

Egg.etym: [OE. eggen, Icel. eggja, fr. egg edge. ��. See Edge.]

senses.d: Pertaining to Egypt, in Africa.

Egyptian.etym: [L. Aegyptius, Gr. �, fr. � (L. Aegyptus) Egypt: cf. F. égyptien. Cf. Gypsy.]

senses.d: A native, or one of the people, of Egypt; also, the Egyptian language.
A gypsy.
An exclamation expressing delight.
An island in a river; an ait.
Seven and one; as, eight years.

Eight.etym: [AS. eahta; akin to OS. ahto, OFries. achta, D. & G. acht, OHG. ahto, Icel. ātta, Sw. åtta, Dan. otte, Goth. ahtau, Lith. asztůni, Ir. & Gael. ochd, W. wyth, Armor. eich, eiz, L. octo, Gr. οκτὤ, Skr. ashṭan. √306. Cf. Octave.]

senses.d: The number greater by a unit than seven; eight units or objects.
A symbol representing eight units, as 8 or viii.
Eight and ten; as, eighteen pounds.

Eighteen.etym: [AS. eahtatȳne, eahtatēne. See Eight, and Ten, and cf. Eighty.]

senses.d: The number greater by a unit than seventeen; eighteen units or objects.
A symbol denoting eighteen units, as 18 or xviii.
Next in order after the seventeenth.
Consisting of one of eighteen equal parts or divisions of a thing.
The quotient of a unit divided by eighteen; one of eighteen equal parts or divisions.
The eighth after the tenth.
Next in order after the seventh.
Consisting of one of eight equal divisions of a thing.
The quotient of a unit divided by eight; one of eight equal parts; an eighth part.
The interval of an octave.
The next in order after seventy-ninth.
Consisting of one of eighty equal parts or divisions.
The quotient of a unit divided by eighty; one of eighty equal parts.
Eight times ten; fourscore.

Eighty.etym: [AS. eahtatig, where the ending -tig is akin to English ten; cf. G. achtzig. See Eight, and Ten.]

senses.d: The sum of eight times ten; eighty units or objects.
A symbol representing eighty units, or ten eight times repeated, as 80 or lxxx.
One of two; the one or the other; — properly used of two things, but sometimes of a larger number, for any one.
q: Lepidus flatters both, Of both is flattered; but he neither loves, Nor either cares for him.
Scarce a palm of ground could be gotten by either of the three.
There have been three talkers in Great British, either of whom would illustrate what I say about dogmatists.

senses.d: Each of two; the one and the other; both; — formerly, also, each of any number.
q: His flowing hair In curls on either cheek played.
On either side . . . was there the tree of life.
The extreme right and left of either army never engaged.

Either.etym: [OE. either, aither, AS. ǣgðer, ǣghwæðer (akin to OHG. ēogiwedar, MHG. iegeweder); ā + ge + hwæðer whether. See Each, and Whether, and cf. Or, conj.]

senses.d: Either precedes two, or more, coördinate words or phrases, and is introductory to an alternative. It is correlative to or.
q: Either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth.
Few writers hesitate to use either in what is called a triple alternative; such as, We must either stay where we are, proceed, or recede.
Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs?

senses.d: To increase; to add to; to augment; — now commonly used with out, the notion conveyed being to add to, or piece out by a laborious, inferior, or scanty addition; as, to eke out a scanty supply of one kind with some other.
q: He eked out by his wits an income of barely fifty pounds.

Eke.etym: [AS. ēkan, ȳkan; akin to OFries, āka, OS. �kian, OHG. ouhhōn to add, Icel. auka to increase, Sw. öka, Dan. öge, Goth. aukan, L. augere, Skr. �jas strength, ugra mighty, and probably to English wax, v. i. Cf. Augment, Nickname.]

senses.d: In addition; also; likewise.
q: 'T will be prodigious hard to prove That this is eke the throne of love.
A trainband captain eke was he Of famous London town.

Eke.etym: [AS. eác; akin to OFries. ák, OS. �k, D. �ok, OHG. ouh, G. auch, Icel. auk, Sw. och and, Dan. og, Goth. auk for, but. Prob. from the preceding verb.]

senses.d: An addition.
q: Clumsy ekes that may well be spared.

senses.d: A dweller in Flam (or Susiana), an ancient kingdom of Southwestern Asia, afterwards a province of Persia.
Old.
Age; esp., old age.
q: As sooth is said, eelde hath great avantage.
Great Nature, ever young, yet full of eld.

senses.d: Old times; former days; antiquity.
q: Astrologers and men of eld.

Eld.etym: [AS. yldu, yldo, eldo, old age, fr. ald, eald, old. See Old.]

senses.d: To age; to grow old.
To make old or ancient.
q: Time, that eldeth all things.

senses.d: Older; more aged, or existing longer.
q: Let the elder men among us emulate their own earlier deeds.

senses.d: Born before another; prior in years; senior; earlier; older; as, his elder brother died in infancy; — opposed to younger, and now commonly applied to a son, daughter, child, brother, etc.
q: The elder shall serve the younger.
But ask of elder days, earth's vernal hour.

Elder.etym: [AS. yldra, compar. of eald old. See Old.]

senses.d: One who is older; a superior in age; a senior.
An aged person; one who lived at an earlier period; a predecessor.
q: Carry your head as your elders have done.

senses.d: A person who, on account of his age, occupies the office of ruler or judge; hence, a person occupying any office appropriate to such as have the experience and dignity which age confers; as, the elders of Israel; the elders of the synagogue; the elders in the apostolic church.
A clergyman authorized to administer all the sacraments; as, a traveling elder.

Elder.etym: [AS. ealdor an elder, prince, fr. eald old. See Old, and cf. Elder, a., Alderman.]

senses.d: A genus of shrubs (Sambucus) having broad umbels of white flowers, and small black or red berries.

Elder.etym: [OE. ellern, eller, AS. ellen, cf. LG. elloorn; perh. akin to OHG. holantar, holuntar, G. holunder; or perh. to E. alder, n.]

senses.d: Oldest; longest in duration.
Born or living first, or before the others, as a son, daughter, brother, etc.; first in origin. See Elder.
q: Their eldest historians are of suspected credit.

Eldest.etym: [AS. yldest, superl. of eald old. See Elder, a.]

senses.d: Chosen; taken by preference from among two or more.
Chosen as the object of mercy or divine favor; set apart to eternal life.
Chosen to an office, but not yet actually inducted into it; as, bishop elect; governor or mayor elect.

Elect.etym: [L. electus, p. p. of eligere to elect; e out + legere to choose. See Legend, and cf. Elite, Eclectic.]

senses.d: One chosen or set apart.
q: Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth.

senses.d: Those who are chosen for salvation.
q: Shall not God avenge his won elect?

senses.d: To pick out; to select; to choose.
q: The deputy elected by the Lord.

senses.d: To select or take for an office; to select by vote; as, to elect a representative, a president, or a governor.
To designate, choose, or select, as an object of mercy or favor.

Elect.syn: To choose; prefer; select. See Choose.

senses.d: The act of choosing; choice; selection.
The act of choosing a person to fill an office, or to membership in a society, as by ballot, uplifted hands, or viva voce; as, the election of a president or a mayor.
q: Corruption in elections is the great enemy of freedom.

senses.d: Power of choosing; free will; liberty to choose or act.
Discriminating choice; discernment.
q: To use men with much difference and election is good.

senses.d: Divine choice; predestination of individuals as objects of mercy and salvation; — one of the “five points” of Calvinism.
q: There is a remnant according to the election of grace.

senses.d: The choice, made by a party, of two alternatives, by taking one of which, the chooser is excluded from the other.
Those who are elected.
q: The election hath obtained it.
He has made his election to walk, in the main, in the old paths.

Election.etym: [F. élection, L. electio, fr. eligere to choose out. See Elect, a.]

senses.d: One of the simplest or essential parts or principles of which anything consists, or upon which the constitution or fundamental powers of anything are based.

One of the ultimate, undecomposable constituents of any kind of matter. Specifically: (Chem.) A substance which cannot be decomposed into different kinds of matter by any means at present employed; as, the elements of water are oxygen and hydrogen.

One of the ultimate parts which are variously combined in anything; as, letters are the elements of written language; hence, also, a simple portion of that which is complex, as a shaft, lever, wheel, or any simple part in a machine; one of the essential ingredients of any mixture; a constituent part; as, quartz, feldspar, and mica are the elements of granite.
q: The simplicity which is so large an element in a noble nature was laughed to scorn.

senses.d: One out of several parts combined in a system of aggregation, when each is of the nature of the whole; as, a single cell is an element of the honeycomb.
One of the simplest essential parts, more commonly called cells, of which animal and vegetable organisms, or their tissues and organs, are composed.

An infinitesimal part of anything of the same nature as the entire magnitude considered; as, in a solid an element may be the infinitesimal portion between any two planes that are separated an indefinitely small distance. In the calculus, element is sometimes used as synonymous with differential.
One of the necessary data or values upon which a system of calculations depends, or general conclusions are based; as, the elements of a planet's orbit.
The simplest or fundamental principles of any system in philosophy, science, or art; rudiments; as, the elements of geometry, or of music.
Any outline or sketch, regarded as containing the fundamental ideas or features of the thing in question; as, the elements of a plan.
One of the simple substances, as supposed by the ancient philosophers; one of the imaginary principles of matter.
q: Of elements The grosser feeds the purer: Earth the Sea; Earth and the Sea feed Air; the Air those Fires Ethereal.
Does not our life consist of the four elements?
And the complexion of the element [i.e.,the sky or air] In favor's like the work we have in hand, Most bloody, fiery, and most terrible.
About twelve ounces , with mere element for drink.
They show that they are out of their element.

senses.d: the conditions and movements of the air.
The elements of the alchemists were salt, sulphur, and mercury.
To compound of elements or first principles.
To constitute; to make up with elements.
q: His very soul was elemented of nothing but sadness.

senses.d: Ten and one added; as, eleven men.

Eleven.etym: [OE. enleven, AS. endleofan, endlufon, for nleofan; akin to LG. eleve, ölwe, ölwen, D. elf, G. elf, eilf, OHG. einlif, Icel. ellifu, Sw. elfva, Dan. elleve, Goth. ainlif, cf. Lith. vënolika; and fr. the root of E. one + (prob.) a root signifying “to be left over, remain,” appearing in E. loan, or pe

senses.d: The sum of ten and one; eleven units or objects.
A symbol representing eleven units, as 11 or xi.
The eleven men selected to play on one side in a match, as the representatives of a club or a locality; as, the all-England eleven.
Next after the tenth; as, the eleventh chapter.
Constituting one of eleven parts into which a thing is divided; as, the eleventh part of a thing.
Of or pertaining to the interval of the octave and the fourth.
The quotient of a unit divided by eleven; one of eleven equal parts.
The interval consisting of ten conjunct degrees; the interval made up of an octave and a fourth.

A tree of the genus Ulmus, of several species, much used as a shade tree, particularly in America. The English elm is Ulmus campestris; the common American or white elm is U. Americana; the slippery or red elm, U. fulva.

Elm.etym: [AS. elm; akin to D. olm, OHG. elm, G. ulme, Icel. almr, Dan. & Sw. alm, L. ulmus, and E. alder. Cf. Old.]

senses.d: Having the power of expressing strong emotions or forcible arguments in an elevated, impassioned, and effective manner; as, an eloquent orator or preacher.
q: O Death, all-eloquent! You only prove What dust we dote on when 't is man we love.

senses.d: Adapted to express strong emotion or to state facts arguments with fluency and power; as, an eloquent address or statement; an eloquent appeal to a jury.

Eloquent.etym: [F. éloquent, L. eloquens, -entis, p. pr. of eloqui to speak out, declaim; e + loqui to speak. See Loquacious.]

senses.d: Other; one or something beside; as, Who else is coming? What else shall I give? Do you expect anything else?

Else.etym: [OE. & AS. elles otherwise, gen. sing. of an adj. signifying other; akin to OHG. elles otherwise, OSw. äljes, Sw. eljest, Goth. aljis, adj., other, L. alius, Gr. �. Cf. Alias, Alien.]

senses.d: Besides; except that mentioned; in addition; as, nowhere else; no one else.
Otherwise; in the other, or the contrary, case; if the facts were different.
q: For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it.

senses.d: The sixth month of the Jewish year, by the sacred reckoning, or the twelfth, by the civil reckoning, corresponding nearly to the month of September.

To anoint all over with balm; especially, to preserve from decay by means of balm or other aromatic oils, or spices; to fill or impregnate (a dead body), with aromatics and drugs that it may resist putrefaction.
q: Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm �is father; and the physicians embalmed Israel.

senses.d: To fill or imbue with sweet odor; to perfume.
q: With fresh dews embalmed the earth.

senses.d: To preserve from decay or oblivion as if with balm; to perpetuate in remembrance.
q: Those tears eternal that embalm the dead.

Embalm.etym: [F. embaumer; pref. em- (L. in) + baume balm. See Balm.]

senses.d: To give boldness or courage to; to encourage.
q: The self-conceit which emboldened him to undertake this dangerous office.

senses.d: To fasten on, as armor.
To clasp in the arms with affection; to take in the arms; to hug.
q: I will embrace him with a soldier's arm, That he shall shrink under my courtesy.
Paul called unto him the disciples, and embraced them.

senses.d: To cling to; to cherish; to love.
To seize eagerly, or with alacrity; to accept with cordiality; to welcome.
q: What is there that he may not embrace for truth?

senses.d: To encircle; to encompass; to inclose.
q: Low at his feet a spacious plain is placed, Between the mountain and the stream embraced.

senses.d: To include as parts of a whole; to comprehend; to take in; as, natural philosophy embraces many sciences.
q: Not that my song, in such a scanty space, So large a subject fully can embrace.

senses.d: To accept; to undergo; to submit to.
To attempt to influence corruptly, as a jury or court.

Embrace.syn: To clasp; hug; inclose; encompass; include; comprise; comprehend; contain; involve; imply.
Embrace.etym: [OE. embracier, F. embrasser; pref. em- (L. in) + F. bras arm. See Brace, n.]

senses.d: To join in an embrace.
Intimate or close encircling with the arms; pressure to the bosom; clasp; hug.
q: We stood tranced in long embraces, Mixed with kisses.

senses.d: To ornament with needlework; as, to embroider a scarf.
q: Thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen.

senses.d: One who embroiders.
A precious stone of a rich green color, a variety of beryl. See Beryl.
A kind of type, in size between minion and nonpare�l. It is used by English printers.

Emerald.etym: [OE. emeraude, OF. esmeraude, esmeralde, F. émeraude, L. smaragdus, fr. Gr. �; cf. �kr. marakata.]

senses.d: Of a rich green color, like that of the emerald.
Hemorrhoids; piles; tumors; boils.
High; lofty; towering; prominent.

Being, metaphorically, above others, whether by birth, high station, merit, or virtue; high in public estimation; distinguished; conspicuous; as, an eminent station; an eminent historian, statements, statesman, or saint.

Eminent.syn: Lofty; elevated; exalted; conspicuous; prominent; remarkable; distinguished; illustrious; famous; celebrated; renowned; well-known. See Distinguished.
Eminent.etym: [L. eminens, -entis, p. pr. of eminere to stand out, be prominent; e out + minere (in comp.) to project; of uncertain origin: cf. F. éminent. Cf. Menace.]

senses.d: Supreme power; sovereignty; sway; dominion.
q: Over hell extend His empire, and with iron scepter rule.

senses.d: The dominion of an emperor; the territory or countries under the jurisdiction and dominion of an emperor (rarely of a king), usually of greater extent than a kingdom, always comprising a variety in the nationality of, or the forms of administration in, constituent and subordinate portions; as, the Austrian empire.
q: Empire carries with it the idea of a vast and complicated government.

senses.d: Any dominion; supreme control; governing influence; rule; sway; as, the empire of mind or of reason.
q: Another force which, in the Middle Ages, shared with chivalry the empire over the minds of men.

Empire.syn: Sway; dominion; rule; control; reign; sovereignty; government; kingdom; realm; state.
Empire.etym: [F., fr. L. imperium a command, sovereignty, dominion, empire, fr. imperare. See Emperor; cf. Imperial.]

senses.d: To inclose; to infold.

To use; to have in service; to cause to be engaged in doing something; — often followed by in, about, on, or upon, and sometimes by to; as: (a) To make use of, as an instrument, a means, a material, etc., for a specific purpose; to apply; as, to employ the pen in writing, bricks in building, words and phrases in speaking; to employ the mind; to employ one's energies.
q: This is a day in which the thoughts . . . ought to be employed on serious subjects.

senses.d: To occupy; as, to employ time in study.
To have or keep at work; to give employment or occupation to; to intrust with some duty or behest; as, to employ a hundred workmen; to employ an envoy.
q: Jonathan . . . and Jahaziah . . . were employed about this matter.
Thy vineyard must employ the sturdy steer To turn the glebe.

Employ.syn: To use; busy; apply; exercise; occupy; engross; engage. See Use.
Employ.etym: [F. employer, fr. L. implicare to fold into, infold, involve, implicate, engage; in + plicare to fold. See Ply, and cf. Imply, Implicate.]

senses.d: That which engages or occupies a person; fixed or regular service or business; employment.
q: The whole employ of body and of mind.

senses.d: The act of employing or using; also, the state of being employed.

That which engages or occupies; that which consumes time or attention; office or post of business; service; as, agricultural employments; mechanical employments; public employments; in the employment of government.
q: Cares are employments, and without employ The soul is on a rack.

Employment.syn: Work; business; occupation; vocation; calling; office; service; commission; trade; profession.

senses.d: One who, or that which, empties.
of Empty.
The state of being empty; absence of contents; void space; vacuum; as, the emptiness of a vessel; emptiness of the stomach.
Want of solidity or substance; unsatisfactoriness; inability to satisfy desire; vacuity; hollowness; the emptiness of earthly glory.
Want of knowledge; lack of sense; vacuity of mind.
q: Eternal smiles his emptiness betray.
The sins of emptiness, gossip, and spite.

senses.d: Containing nothing; not holding or having anything within; void of contents or appropriate contents; not filled; — said of an inclosure, as a box, room, house, etc.; as, an empty chest, room, purse, or pitcher; an empty stomach; empty shackles.
Free; clear; devoid; — often with of.
q: I shall find you empty of that fault.

senses.d: Having nothing to carry; unburdened.
q: When ye go ye shall not go empty.

senses.d: Destitute of effect, sincerity, or sense; — said of language; as, empty words, or threats.
q: Words are but empty thanks.

senses.d: Unable to satisfy; unsatisfactory; hollow; vain; — said of pleasure, the world, etc.
q: Pleas'd in the silent shade with empty praise.

senses.d: Producing nothing; unfruitful; — said of a plant or tree; as, an empty vine.
q: Seven empty ears blasted with the east wind.

senses.d: Destitute of, or lacking, sense, knowledge, or courtesy; as, empty brains; an empty coxcomb.
q: That in civility thou seem'st so empty.

senses.d: Destitute of reality, or real existence; unsubstantial; as, empty dreams.

Empty.etym: [AS. emtig, æmtig, æmetig, fr. æmta, æmetta, quiet, leisure, rest; of uncertain origin; cf. G. emsig busy.]

senses.d: An empty box, crate, cask, etc.; — used in commerce, esp. in transportation of freight; as, “special rates for empties.”
To deprive of the contents; to exhaust; to make void or destitute; to make vacant; to pour out; to discharge; as, to empty a vessel; to empty a well or a cistern.
q: The clouds . . . empty themselves upon the earth.

senses.d: To discharge itself; as, a river empties into the ocean.
To become empty.
The endeavor to equal or to excel another in qualities or actions; an assiduous striving to equal or excel another; rivalry.
q: A noble emulation heats your breast.

senses.d: Jealous rivalry; envy; envious contention.
q: Such factious emulations shall arise.

Emulation.syn: Competition; rivalry; contest; contention; strife. — Emulation, Competition, Rivalry. Competition is the struggle of two or more persons for the same object. Emulation is an ardent desire for superiority, arising from competition, but now implying, of necessity, any improper feeling. Rivalry is a personal contest, and, almost of course, has a selfish object and gives rise to envy. “Competition and emulation have honor for their basis; rivalry is but a desire for selfish gratification. senses.d: Half an em, that is, half of the unit of space in measuring printed matter. See Em.
To give strength or ability to; to make firm and strong.
q: Receive the Holy Ghost, said Christ to his apostles, when he enabled them with priestly power.

senses.d: To make able (to do, or to be, something); to confer sufficient power upon; to furnish with means, opportunities, and the like; to render competent for; to empower; to endow.
q: Temperance gives Nature her full play, and enables her to exert herself in all her force and vigor.

senses.d: To form and occupy a camp; to prepare and settle in temporary habitations, as tents or huts; to halt on a march, pitch tents, or form huts, and remain for the night or for a longer time, as an army or a company traveling.
q: The host of the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim.

senses.d: To form into a camp; to place in a temporary habitation, or quarters.
q: Bid him encamp his soldiers.

senses.d: To charm by sorcery; to act on by enchantment; to get control of by magical words and rites.
q: And now about the caldron sing, Like elves and fairies in a ring, Enchanting all that you put in.
He is enchanted, cannot speak.

senses.d: To delight in a high degree; to charm; to enrapture; as, music enchants the ear.
q: Arcadia was the charmed circle where all his spirits forever should be enchanted.

Enchant.syn: To charm; bewitch; fascinate. Cf. Charm.
Enchant.etym: [F. enchanter, L. incantare to chant or utter a magic formula over or against one, to bewitch; in in, against + cantare to sing. See Chant, and cf. Incantation.]

senses.d: One who enchants; a sorcerer or magician; also, one who delights as by an enchantment.
q: Like ghosts from an enchanter fleeing.

senses.d: The act of enchanting; the production of certain wonderful effects by the aid of demons, or the agency of supposed spirits; the use of magic arts, spells, or charms; incantation.
q: After the last enchantment you did here.

senses.d: The effect produced by the act; the state of being enchanted; as, to break an enchantment.
That which captivates the heart and senses; an influence or power which fascinates or highly delights.
q: Such an enchantment as there is in words.

Enchantment.syn: Incantation; necromancy; magic; sorcery; witchcraft; spell; charm; fascination; witchery.

senses.d: To come against face to face; to meet; to confront, either by chance, suddenly, or deliberately; especially, to meet in opposition or with hostile intent; to engage in conflict with; to oppose; to struggle with; as, to encounter a friend in traveling; two armies encounter each other; to encounter obstacles or difficulties, to encounter strong evidence of a truth.
q: Then certain philosophers of the Epicureans, and of the Stoics, encountered him.
I am most fortunate thus accidentally to encounter you.

Encounter.etym: [OF. encontrer; pref. en- (L. in) + contre against, L. contra. See Counter, adv.]

senses.d: To meet face to face; to have a meeting; to meet, esp. as enemies; to engage in combat; to fight; as, three armies encountered at Waterloo.
q: I will encounter with Andronicus.
Perception and judgment, employed in the investigation of all truth, have in the first place to encounter with particulars.

senses.d: A meeting face to face; a running against; a sudden or incidental meeting; an interview.
q: To shun the encounter of the vulgar crowd.

senses.d: A meeting, with hostile purpose; hence, a combat; a battle; as, a bloody encounter.
q: As one for . . . fierce encounters fit
To join their dark encounter in mid-air

Encounter.syn: Contest; conflict; fight; combat; assault; rencounter; attack; engagement; onset. See Contest.
Encounter.etym: [OF. encontre, fr. encontrer. See Encounter, v. t.]

senses.d: To give courage to; to inspire with courage, spirit, or hope; to raise, or to increase, the confidence of; to animate; enhearten; to incite; to help forward; — the opposite of discourage.
q: David encouraged himself in the Lord.

Encourage.syn: To embolden; inspirit; animate; enhearten; hearten; incite; cheer; urge; impel; stimulate; instigate; countenance; comfort; promote; advance; forward; strengthen.
Encourage.etym: [F. encourager; pref. en- (L. in) + courage courage. See Courage.]

senses.d: The extreme or last point or part of any material thing considered lengthwise (the extremity of breadth being side); hence, extremity, in general; the concluding part; termination; close; limit; as, the end of a field, line, pole, road; the end of a year, of a discourse; put an end to pain; — opposed to beginning, when used of anything having a first part.
q: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof.

senses.d: Point beyond which no procession can be made; conclusion; issue; result, whether successful or otherwise; conclusive event; consequence.
q: My guilt be on my head, and there an end.
O that a man might know The end of this day's business ere it come!

senses.d: Termination of being; death; destruction; extermination; also, cause of death or destruction.
q: Unblamed through life, lamented in thy end.
Confound your hidden falsehood, and award Either of you to be the other's end.
I shall see an end of him.

senses.d: The object aimed at in any effort considered as the close and effect of exertion; ppurpose; intention; aim; as, to labor for private or public ends.
q: Losing her, the end of living lose.
When every man is his own end, all things will come to a bad end.

senses.d: That which is left; a remnant; a fragment; a scrap; as, odds and ends.
q: I clothe my naked villainy With old odd ends stolen out of holy writ, And seem a saint, when most I play the devil.

senses.d: One of the yarns of the worsted warp in a Brussels carpet.

End.etym: [OE. & AS. ende; akin to OS. endi, D. einde, eind, OHG. enti, G. ende, Icel. endir, endi, Sw. ände, Dan. ende, Goth. andeis, Skr. anta. √208. Cf. Ante-, Anti-, Answer.]

senses.d: To bring to an end or conclusion; to finish; to close; to terminate; as, to end a speech.
q: On the seventh day God ended his work.

senses.d: To form or be at the end of; as, the letter k ends the word back.
To destroy; to put to death.
To come to the ultimate point; to be finished; to come to a close; to cease; to terminate; as, a voyage ends; life ends; winter ends.
To bring loss or damage to; to harm; to injure.
q: The trial hath endamaged thee no way.

senses.d: To put to hazard; to bring into danger or peril; to expose to loss or injury; as, to endanger life or peace.
q: All the other difficulties of his reign only exercised without endangering him.

senses.d: To incur the hazard of; to risk.
q: He that turneth the humors back . . . endangereth malign ulcers.

senses.d: Termination; concluding part; result; conclusion; destruction; death.
The final syllable or letter of a word; the part joined to the stem. See 3d Case, 5.
Without end; having no end or conclusion; perpetual; interminable; — applied to length, and to duration; as, an endless line; endless time; endless bliss; endless praise; endless clamor.
Infinite; excessive; unlimited.
Without profitable end; fruitless; unsatisfying.
Void of design; objectless; as, an endless pursuit.

Endless.syn: Eternal; everlasting; interminable; infinite; unlimited; incessant; perpetual; uninterrupted; continual; unceasing; unending; boundless; undying; imperishable.

senses.d: To furnish with money or its equivalent, as a permanent fund for support; to make pecuniary provision for; to settle an income upon; especially, to furnish with dower; as, to endow a wife; to endow a public institution.
q: Endowing hospitals and almshouses.

senses.d: To enrich or furnish with anything of the nature of a gift (as a quality or faculty); — followed by with, rarely by of; as, man is endowed by his Maker with reason; to endow with privileges or benefits.

Endow.etym: [OF. endouer; pref. en- (L. in) + F. douer to endow, L. dotare. See Dower, and cf. 2d Endue.]

senses.d: To invest.
q: Tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high.
Endue them . . . with heavenly gifts.

Endue.etym: [L. induere, prob. confused with E. endow. See Indue.]

senses.d: An older spelling of Endow.
To continue in the same state without perishing; to last; to remain.
q: Their verdure still endure.
He shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure.

senses.d: To remain firm, as under trial or suffering; to suffer patiently or without yielding; to bear up under adversity; to hold out.
q: Can thine heart endure, or can thine hands be strong in the days that I shall deal with thee?

Endure.etym: [F. endurer; pref. en- (L. in) + durer to last. See Dure, v. i., and cf. Indurate.]

senses.d: To remain firm under; to sustain; to undergo; to support without breaking or yielding; as, metals endure a certain degree of heat without melting; to endure wind and weather.
q: Both were of shining steel, and wrought so pure, As might the strokes of two such arms endure.

senses.d: To bear with patience; to suffer without opposition or without sinking under the pressure or affliction; to bear up under; to put up with; to tolerate.
q: I will no longer endure it.
Therefore I endure all things for the elect's sake.
How can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people?

senses.d: To harden; to toughen; to make hardy.
q: Manly limbs endured with little ease.

Endure.syn: To last; remain; continue; abide; brook; submit to; suffer.

senses.d: Lasting; durable; long-suffering; as, an enduring disposition.
One hostile to another; one who hates, and desires or attempts the injury of, another; a foe; an adversary; as, an enemy of or to a person; an enemy to truth, or to falsehood.
q: To all good he enemy was still.
I say unto you, Love your enemies.

Enemy.etym: [OF. enemi, F. ennemi, from L. inimicus; in- (negative) + amicus friend. See Amicable.]

senses.d: Hostile; inimical.
q: They . . . every day grow more enemy to God.

senses.d: To put under pledge; to pledge; to place under obligations to do or forbear doing something, as by a pledge, oath, or promise; to bind by contract or promise.
To gain for service; to bring in as associate or aid; to enlist; as, to engage friends to aid in a cause; to engage men for service.
To gain over; to win and attach; to attract and hold; to draw.
q: Good nature engages everybody to him.

senses.d: To employ the attention and efforts of; to occupy; to engross; to draw on.
q: Thus shall mankind his guardian care engage.
Taking upon himself the difficult task of engaging him in conversation.

senses.d: To enter into contest with; to encounter; to bring to conflict.
q: A favorable opportunity of engaging the enemy.

senses.d: To come into gear with; as, the teeth of one cogwheel engage those of another, or one part of a clutch engages the other part.

Engage.etym: [F. engager; pref. en- (L. in) + gage pledge, pawn. See Gage.]

senses.d: To promise or pledge one's self; to enter into an obligation; to become bound; to warrant.
q: How proper the remedy for the malady, I engage not.

senses.d: To embark in a business; to take a part; to employ or involve one's self; to devote attention and effort; to enlist; as, to engage in controversy.
To enter into conflict; to join battle; as, the armies engaged in a general battle.
To be in gear, as two cogwheels working together.
Occupied; employed; busy.
Pledged; promised; especially, having the affections pledged; promised in marriage; affianced; betrothed.
Greatly interested; of awakened zeal; earnest.
Involved; esp., involved in a hostile encounter; as, the engaged ships continued the fight.
(Pronounced, in this sense, ����.) Natural capacity; ability; skill.
q: A man hath sapiences three, Memory, engine, and intellect also.

senses.d: Anything used to effect a purpose; any device or contrivance; an agent.
q: You see the ways the fisherman doth take To catch the fish; what engines doth he make?
Their promises, enticements, oaths, tokens, and all these engines of lust.

senses.d: Any instrument by which any effect is produced; especially, an instrument or machine of war or torture.
A compound machine by which any physical power is applied to produce a given physical effect.

Engine.etym: [F. engin skill, machine, engine, L. ingenium natural capacity, invention; in in + the root of gignere to produce. See Genius, and cf. Ingenious, Gin a snare.]

senses.d: To assault with an engine.
q: To engine and batter our walls.

senses.d: To equip with an engine; — said especially of steam vessels; as, vessels are often built by one firm and engined by another.
(Pronounced, in this sense, �����.) To rack; to torture.
To deposit in the grave; to bury.

Engrave.etym: [Pref. en- + grave a tomb. Cf. Engrave to carve.]

senses.d: To cut in; to make by incision.
q: Full many wounds in his corrupted flesh He did engrave.

senses.d: To cut with a graving instrument in order to form an inscription or pictorial representation; to carve figures; to mark with incisions.
q: Like . . . . a signet thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel.

senses.d: To form or represent by means of incisions upon wood, stone, metal, or the like; as, to engrave an inscription.
To impress deeply; to infix, as if with a graver.
q: Engrave principles in men's minds.

Engrave.etym: [Pref. en- + grave to carve: cf. OF. engraver.]

senses.d: One who engraves; a person whose business it is to produce engraved work, especially on metal or wood.

The act or art of producing upon hard material incised or raised patterns, characters, lines, and the like; especially, the art of producing such lines, etc., in the surface of metal plates or blocks of wood. Engraving is used for the decoration of the surface itself; also, for producing an original, from which a pattern or design may be printed on paper.
That which is engraved; an engraved plate.
An impression from an engraved plate, block of wood, or other material; a print.
To lay upon, as an order or command; to give an injunction to; to direct with authority; to order; to charge.
q: High matter thou enjoin'st me.
I am enjoined by oath to observe three things.

senses.d: To prohibit or restrain by a judicial order or decree; to put an injunction on.
q: This is a suit to enjoin the defendants from disturbing the plaintiffs.

Enjoin.etym: [F. enjoindre, L. injungere to join into, charge, enjoin; in + jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Injunction.]

senses.d: To join or unite.
To take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of; to feel or perceive with pleasure; to be delighted with; as, to enjoy the dainties of a feast; to enjoy conversation.
To have, possess, and use with satisfaction; to occupy or have the benefit of, as a good or profitable thing, or as something desirable; as, to enjoy a free constitution and religious liberty.
q: That the children of Israel may enjoy every man the inheritance of his fathers.
To enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season.

senses.d: To have sexual intercourse with.

Enjoy.etym: [OF. enjoier to receive with joy; pref. en- (L. in) + OF. & F. joie joy: cf. OF. enjoir to enjoy. See Joy.]

senses.d: To take satisfaction; to live in happiness.
To make larger; to increase in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits; to magnify; as, the body is enlarged by nutrition; to enlarge one's house.
q: To enlarge their possessions of land.

senses.d: To increase the capacity of; to expand; to give free scope or greater scope to; also, to dilate, as with joy, affection, and the like; as, knowledge enlarges the mind.
q: O ye Corinthians, our . . . heart is enlarged.

senses.d: To set at large or set free.
q: It will enlarge us from all restraints.

Enlarge.syn: To increase; extend; expand; spread; amplify; augment; magnify. See Increase.
Enlarge.etym: [OF. enlargier; pref. en- (L. in) + F. large wide. See Large.]

senses.d: To grow large or larger; to be further extended; to expand; as, a plant enlarges by growth; an estate enlarges by good management; a volume of air enlarges by rarefaction.
To speak or write at length; to be diffuse in speaking or writing; to expatiate; to dilate.
q: To enlarge upon this theme.

senses.d: To get more astern or parallel with the vessel's course; to draw aft; — said of the wind.
Made large or larger; extended; swollen.
The act of increasing in size or bulk, real or apparent; the state of being increased; augmentation; further extension; expansion.
Expansion or extension, as of the powers of the mind; ennoblement, as of the feelings and character; as, an enlargement of views, of knowledge, of affection.
A setting at large, or being set at large; release from confinement, servitude, or distress; liberty.
q: Give enlargement to the swain.

senses.d: Diffusiveness of speech or writing; expatiation; a wide range of discourse or argument.
q: An enlargement upon the vices and corruptions that were got into the army.

senses.d: To supply with light; to illuminate; as, the sun enlightens the earth.
q: His lightnings enlightened the world.

senses.d: To make clear to the intellect or conscience; to shed the light of truth and knowledge upon; to furnish with increase of knowledge; to instruct; as, to enlighten the mind or understanding.
q: The conscience enlightened by the Word and Spirit of God.

Enlighten.etym: [Pref. en- + lighten: cf. AS. inlīhtan. Cf. Enlight.]

senses.d: The quality of being an enemy; hostile or unfriendly disposition.
q: No ground of enmity between us known.

senses.d: A state of opposition; hostility.
q: The friendship of the world is enmity with God.

Enmity.syn: Rancor; hostility; hatred; aversion; antipathy; repugnance; animosity; ill will; malice; malevolence. See Animosity, Rancor.
Enmity.etym: [OE. enemyte, fr. enemy: cf. F. inimitié, OF. enemistié. See Enemy, and cf. Amity.]

senses.d: Satisfying desire; giving content; adequate to meet the want; sufficient; — usually, and more elegantly, following the noun to which it belongs.
q: How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare!

Enough.etym: [OE. inoh, inow, enogh, AS. genōh, genōg, a. & adv. (akin to OS. ginōg, D. genoeg, OHG. ginoug, G. genug, Icel. gnōgr, Sw. nog, Dan. nok, Goth. ganōhs), fr. geneah it suffices (akin to Goth. ganah); pref. ge- + a root akin to L. nancisci to get, Skr. naç, Gr. ενεγκεἰ̑ν to carry.]

senses.d: In a degree or quantity that satisfies; to satisfaction; sufficiently.
Fully; quite; — used to express slight augmentation of the positive degree, and sometimes equivalent to very; as, he is ready enough to embrace the offer.
q: I know you well enough; you are Signior Antonio.
Thou knowest well enough . . . that this is no time to lend money.

senses.d: In a tolerable degree; — used to express mere acceptableness or acquiescence, and implying a degree or quantity rather less than is desired; as, the song was well enough.
A sufficiency; a quantity which satisfies desire, is adequate to the want, or is equal to the power or ability; as, he had enough to do take care of himself.
q: And Esau said, I have enough, my brother.

senses.d: An exclamation denoting sufficiency, being a shortened form of it is enough.
To make rich with any kind of wealth; to render opulent; to increase the possessions of; as, to enrich the understanding with knowledge.
q: Seeing, Lord, your great mercy Us hath enriched so openly.

senses.d: To supply with ornament; to adorn; as, to enrich a ceiling by frescoes.
To make rich with manure; to fertilize; — said of the soil; as, to enrich land by irrigation.
To supply with knowledge; to instruct; to store; — said of the mind.

Enrich.etym: [F. enrichir; pref. en- (L. in) + riche rich. See Rich.]

senses.d: An example; a pattern or model for imitation.
q: Being ensamples to the flock.

Ensample.etym: [OF. ensample, essample, F. exemple. See Example.]

senses.d: To exemplify, to show by example.

A flag; a banner; a standard; esp., the national flag, or a banner indicating nationality, carried by a ship or a body of soldiers; — as distinguished from flags indicating divisions of the army, rank of naval officers, or private signals, and the like.
q: Hang up your ensigns, let your drums be still.

senses.d: A signal displayed like a standard, to give notice.
q: He will lift an ensign to the nations from far.

senses.d: Sign; badge of office, rank, or power; symbol.
q: The ensigns of our power about we bear.

senses.d: Formerly, a commissioned officer of the army who carried the ensign or flag of a company or regiment.

Ensign.etym: [L. enseigne, L. insignia, pl. of insigne a distinctive mark, badge, flag; in + signum mark, sign. See Sign, and cf. Insignia, 3d Ancient.]

senses.d: To designate as by an ensign.
q: Henry but joined the roses that ensigned Particular families.

senses.d: To distinguish by a mark or ornament; esp. (Her.), by a crown; thus, any charge which has a crown immediately above or upon it, is said to be ensigned.
To catch in a snare. See Insnare.
To follow; to pursue; to follow and overtake.
q: To ensue his example in doing the like mischief.

Ensue.etym: [OF. ensevre, OF. & F. ensuivre, fr. L. insequi; in + sequi to pursue. See Sue.]

senses.d: To follow or come afterward; to follow as a consequence or in chronological succession; to result; as, an ensuing conclusion or effect; the year ensuing was a cold one.
q: So spoke the Dame, but no applause ensued.
Damage to the mind or the body, or to both, ensues, unless the exciting cause be presently removed.

Ensue.syn: To follow; pursue; succeed. See Follow.

senses.d: To twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated; to make tangled, confused, and intricate; as, to entangle yarn or the hair.

To involve in such complications as to render extrication a bewildering difficulty; hence, metaphorically, to insnare; to perplex; to bewilder; to puzzle; as, to entangle the feet in a net, or in briers.
q: The difficulties that perplex men's thoughts and entangle their understandings.
Allowing her to entangle herself with a person whose future was so uncertain.

senses.d: To come or go into; to pass into the interior of; to pass within the outer cover or shell of; to penetrate; to pierce; as, to enter a house, a closet, a country, a door, etc.; the river enters the sea.
q: That darksome cave they enter.
I, . . . with the multitude of my redeemed, Shall enter heaven, long absent.

senses.d: To unite in; to join; to be admitted to; to become a member of; as, to enter an association, a college, an army.
To engage in; to become occupied with; as, to enter the legal profession, the book trade, etc.
To pass within the limits of; to attain; to begin; to commence upon; as, to enter one's teens, a new era, a new dispensation.

To cause to go (into), or to be received (into); to put in; to insert; to cause to be admitted; as, to enter a knife into a piece of wood, a wedge into a log; to enter a boy at college, a horse for a race, etc.

To inscribe; to enroll; to record; as, to enter a name, or a date, in a book, or a book in a catalogue; to enter the particulars of a sale in an account, a manifest of a ship or of merchandise at the customhouse.
To go into or upon, as lands, and take actual possession of them.

To make report of (a vessel or her cargo) at the customhouse; to submit a statement of (imported goods), with the original invoices, to the proper officer of the customs for estimating the duties. See Entry, 4.
To file or inscribe upon the records of the land office the required particulars concerning (a quantity of public land) in order to entitle a person to a right of preëmption.
To deposit for copyright the title or description of (a book, picture, map, etc.); as, “entered according to act of Congress.”
To initiate; to introduce favorably.

Enter.etym: [OE. entren, enteren, F. entrer, fr. L. intrare, fr. intro inward, contr. fr. intero (sc. loco), fr. inter in between, between. See Inter-, In, and cf. Interior.]

senses.d: To go or come in; — often with in used pleonastically; also, to begin; to take the first steps.
q: No evil thing approach nor enter in.
Truth is fallen in the street, and equity can not enter.
For we which have believed do enter into rest.

senses.d: To get admission; to introduce one's self; to penetrate; to form or constitute a part; to become a partaker or participant; to share; to engage; — usually with into; sometimes with on or upon; as, a ball enters into the body; water enters into a ship; he enters into the plan; to enter into a quarrel; a merchant enters into partnership with some one; to enter upon another's land; the boy enters on his tenth year; to enter upon a task; lead enters into the composition of pewter.
To penetrate mentally; to consider attentively; — with into.
q: He is particularly pleased with . . . Sallust for his entering into internal principles of action.

senses.d: That which is undertaken; something attempted to be performed; a work projected which involves activity, courage, energy, and the like; a bold, arduous, or hazardous attempt; an undertaking; as, a manly enterprise; a warlike enterprise.
q: Their hands can not perform their enterprise.

senses.d: Willingness or eagerness to engage in labor which requires boldness, promptness, energy, and like qualities; as, a man of great enterprise.

Enterprise.etym: [F. enterprise, fr. entreprendre to undertake; entre between (L. inter) + prendre to take. See Inter, and Emprise.]

senses.d: To undertake; to begin and attempt to perform; to venture upon.
q: The business must be enterprised this night.
What would I not renounce or enterprise for you!

senses.d: To treat with hospitality; to entertain.
q: Him at the threshold met, and well did enterprise.

senses.d: To undertake an enterprise, or something hazardous or difficult.
To be at the charges of; to take or keep in one's service; to maintain; to support; to harbor; to keep.
q: You, sir, I entertain for one of my hundred.

senses.d: To give hospitable reception and maintenance to; to receive at one's board, or into one's house; to receive as a guest.
q: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers; for thereby some have entertained unawares.

senses.d: To engage the attention of agreeably; to amuse with that which makes the time pass pleasantly; to divert; as, to entertain friends with conversation, etc.
q: The weary time she can not entertain.

senses.d: To give reception to; to receive, in general; to receive and take into consideration; to admit, treat, or make use of; as, to entertain a proposal.
q: I am not here going to entertain so large a theme as the philosophy of Locke.
A rumor gained ground, — and, however absurd, was entertained by some very sensible people.

senses.d: To meet or encounter, as an enemy.
To keep, hold, or maintain in the mind with favor; to keep in the mind; to harbor; to cherish; as, to entertain sentiments.
To lead on; to bring along; to introduce.
q: To baptize all nations, and entertain them into the services institutions of the holy Jesus.

Entertain.syn: To amuse; divert; maintain. See Amuse.
Entertain.etym: [F. entretenir; entre between (L. inter) + tenir to hold, L. tenere. See Tenable.]

senses.d: To receive, or provide entertainment for, guests; as, he entertains generously.
Entertainment.

To draw on, by exciting hope or desire; to allure; to attract; as, the bait enticed the fishes. Often in a bad sense: To lead astray; to induce to evil; to tempt; as, the sirens enticed them to listen.
q: Roses blushing as they blow, And enticing men to pull.
My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.
Go, and thine erring brother gain, Entice him home to be forgiven.

Entice.syn: To allure; lure; coax; decoy; seduce; tempt; inveigle; incite; persuade; prevail on. See Allure.
Entice.etym: [OE. entisen, enticen, OF. enticier, entichier; pref. en- (L. in) + a word of uncertain origin, cf. OF. atisier to stir a fire, provoke, L. titio firebrand, or MHG. zicken to push.]

senses.d: That entices; alluring.
Complete in all parts; undivided; undiminished; whole; full and perfect; not deficient; as, the entire control of a business; entire confidence, ignorance.
q: That ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.
With strength entire and free will armed.
One entire and perfect chrysolite.

senses.d: Without mixture or alloy of anything; unqualified; morally whole; pure; faithful.
q: Pure fear and entire cowardice.
No man had ever a heart more entire to the king.

senses.d: Consisting of a single piece, as a corolla.
Not gelded; — said of a horse.
Internal; interior.

Entire.etym: [F. entier, L. integer untouched, undiminished, entire; pref. in-, negative + the root of tangere to touch. See Tangent, and cf. Integer.]

senses.d: Entirely.
A name originally given to a kind of beer combining qualities of different kinds of beer.

The act of entering or going into; ingress; as, the entrance of a person into a house or an apartment; hence, the act of taking possession, as of property, or of office; as, the entrance of an heir upon his inheritance, or of a magistrate into office.
Liberty, power, or permission to enter; as, to give entrance to friends.
The passage, door, or gate, for entering.
q: Show us, we pray thee, the entrance into the city.

senses.d: The entering upon; the beginning, or that with which the beginning is made; the commencement; initiation; as, a difficult entrance into business.
q: St. Augustine, in the entrance of one of his discourses, makes a kind of apology.

senses.d: The causing to be entered upon a register, as a ship or goods, at a customhouse; an entering; as, his entrance of the arrival was made the same day.
The angle which the bow of a vessel makes with the water at the water line.

Entrance.etym: [OF. entrance, fr. OF. & F. entrant, p. pr. of entrer to enter. See Enter.]

senses.d: To put into a trance; to make insensible to present objects.
q: Him, still entranced and in a litter laid, They bore from field and to the bed conveyed.

senses.d: To put into an ecstasy; to ravish with delight or wonder; to enrapture; to charm.
q: And I so ravished with her heavenly note, I stood entranced, and had no room for thought.

senses.d: To treat, or conduct toward; to deal with; to use.
q: Fairly let her be entreated.
I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well.

senses.d: To treat with, or in respect to, a thing desired; hence, to ask earnestly; to beseech; to petition or pray with urgency; to supplicate; to importune.
q: I must entreat of you some of that money.
Some late visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door.
Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife.

senses.d: To beseech or supplicate successfully; to prevail upon by prayer or solicitation; to persuade.
q: It were a fruitless attempt to appease a power whom no prayers could entreat.

senses.d: To invite; to entertain.

Entreat.syn: To beseech; beg; solicit; crave; implore; supplicate. See Beseech.
Entreat.etym: [OE. entreten to treat, request, OF. entraiter to treat of; pref. en- (L. in) + traitier to treat. See Treat.]

senses.d: To treat or discourse; hence, to enter into negotiations, as for a treaty.
q: Of which I shall have further occasion to entreat.
Alexander . . . was first that entreated of true peace with them.

senses.d: To make an earnest petition or request.
q: The Janizaries entreated for them as valiant men.

senses.d: Entreaty.

The act of entering or passing into or upon; entrance; ingress; hence, beginnings or first attempts; as, the entry of a person into a house or city; the entry of a river into the sea; the entry of air into the blood; an entry upon an undertaking.
The act of making or entering a record; a setting down in writing the particulars, as of a transaction; as, an entry of a sale; also, that which is entered; an item.
q: A notary made an entry of this act.

senses.d: That by which entrance is made; a passage leading into a house or other building, or to a room; a vestibule; an adit, as of a mine.
q: A straight, long entry to the temple led.

senses.d: The exhibition or depositing of a ship's papers at the customhouse, to procure license to land goods; or the giving an account of a ship's cargo to the officer of the customs, and obtaining his permission to land the goods. See Enter, v. t., 8, and Entrance, n., 5.
The actual taking possession of lands or tenements, by entering or setting foot on them.

Entry.etym: [OE. entree, entre, F. entrée, fr. entrer to enter. See Enter, and cf. Entrée.]

senses.d: To vie; to emulate; to strive.
Malignant; mischievous; spiteful.
q: Each envious brier his weary legs doth scratch.
