senses.d: Feeling or exhibiting envy; actuated or directed by, or proceeding from, envy; — said of a person, disposition, feeling, act, etc.; jealously pained by the excellence or good fortune of another; maliciously grudging; — followed by of, at, and against; as, an envious man, disposition, attack; envious tongues.
q: My soul is envious of mine eye.
Neither be thou envious at the wicked.

senses.d: Inspiring envy.
q: He to him leapt, and that same envious gage Of victor's glory from him snatched away.

senses.d: Excessively careful; cautious.
q: No men are so envious of their health.

Envious.etym: [OF. envios, F. envieux, fr. L. invidiosus, fr. invidia envy. See Envy, and cf. Invidious.]

senses.d: To surround; to encompass; to encircle; to hem in; to be round about; to involve or envelop.
q: Dwelling in a pleasant glade, With mountains round about environed.
Environed he was with many foes.
Environ me with darkness whilst I write.

Environ.etym: [F. environner, fr. environ about, thereabout; pref. en- (L. in) + OF. viron circle, circuit, fr. OF. & F. virer to turn, LL. virare to turn up and down, topsy-turvy. Cf. Veer.]

senses.d: About; around.
q: Lord Godfrey's eye three times environ goes.

senses.d: Malice; ill will; spite.
q: If he evade us there, Enforce him with his envy to the people.

senses.d: Chagrin, mortification, discontent, or uneasiness at the sight of another's excellence or good fortune, accompanied with some degree of hatred and a desire to possess equal advantages; malicious grudging; — usually followed by of; as, they did this in envy of Cæsar.
q: Envy is a repining at the prosperity or good of another, or anger and displeasure at any good of another which we want, or any advantage another hath above us.
No bliss Enjoyed by us excites his envy more.
Envy, to which the ignoble mind's a slave, Is emulation in the learned or brave.

senses.d: Emulation; rivalry.
q: Such as cleanliness and decency Prompt to a virtuous envy.

senses.d: Public odium; ill repute.
q: To lay the envy of the war upon Cicero.

senses.d: An object of envious notice or feeling.
q: This constitution in former days used to be the envy of the world.

Envy.etym: [F. envie, L. invidia envious; akin to invidere to look askance at, to look with enmity; in against + videre to see. See Vision.]

senses.d: To feel envy at or towards; to be envious of; to have a feeling of uneasiness or mortification in regard to (any one), arising from the sight of another's excellence or good fortune and a longing to possess it.
q: A woman does not envy a man for his fighting courage, nor a man a woman for her beauty.
Whoever envies another confesses his superiority.

senses.d: To feel envy on account of; to have a feeling of grief or repining, with a longing to possess (some excellence or good fortune of another, or an equal good fortune, etc.); to look with grudging upon; to begrudge.
q: I have seen thee fight, When I have envied thy behavior.
Jeffrey . . . had actually envied his friends their cool mountain breezes.

senses.d: To long after; to desire strongly; to covet.
q: Or climb his knee the envied kiss to share.

senses.d: To do harm to; to injure; to disparage.
q: If I make a lie To gain your love and envy my best mistress, Put me against a wall.

senses.d: To hate.
To emulate.
To be filled with envious feelings; to regard anything with grudging and longing eyes; — used especially with at.
q: Who would envy at the prosperity of the wicked?

senses.d: To show malice or ill will; to rail.
A Hebrew dry measure, supposed to be equal to two pecks and five quarts. ten ephahs make one homer.
Of or pertaining to Ephesus, an ancient city of Ionia, in Asia Minor.
A native of Ephesus.
A jolly companion; a roisterer.

A part of the sacerdotal habit among Jews, being a covering for the back and breast, held together on the shoulders by two clasps or brooches of onyx stones set in gold, and fastened by a girdle of the same stuff as the ephod. The ephod for the priests was of plain linen; that for the high priest was richly embroidered in colors. The breastplate of the high priest was worn upon the ephod in front.
A hunter's name for the grizzly bear.
Pertaining to Epicurus, or following his philosophy.
Given to luxury; adapted to luxurious tastes; luxurious; pertaining to good eating.
q: Courses of the most refined and epicurean dishes.

senses.d: A follower or Epicurus.
One given to epicurean indulgence.
A writing directed or sent to a person or persons; a written communication; a letter; — applied usually to formal, didactic, or elegant letters.
q: A madman's epistles are no gospels.

senses.d: One of the letters in the New Testament which were addressed to their Christian brethren by Apostles.
q: One sees the pulpit on the epistle side.

Epistle.etym: [OE. epistle, epistel, AS. epistol, pistol, L. epistola, fr. Gr. � anything sent by a messenger, message, letter, fr. � to send to, tell by letter or message; επἴ upon, to + � to dispatch, send; cf. OF. epistle, epistre, F. épître. See Stall.]

senses.d: To write; to communicate in a letter or by writing.

Agreeing in quantity, size, quality, degree, value, etc.; having the same magnitude, the same value, the same degree, etc.; — applied to number, degree, quantity, and intensity, and to any subject which admits of them; neither inferior nor superior, greater nor less, better nor worse; corresponding; alike; as, equal quantities of land, water, etc. ; houses of equal size; persons of equal stature or talents; commodities of equal value.
Bearing a suitable relation; of just proportion; having competent power, abilities, or means; adequate; as, he is not equal to the task.
q: The Scots trusted not their own numbers as equal to fight with the English.
It is not permitted to me to make my commendations equal to your merit.
Whose voice an equal messenger Conveyed thy meaning mild.

senses.d: Not variable; equable; uniform; even; as, an equal movement.
Evenly balanced; not unduly inclining to either side; characterized by fairness; unbiased; impartial; equitable; just.
q: Are not my ways equal?
Thee, O Jove, no equal judge I deem.
Nor think it equal to answer deliberate reason with sudden heat and noise.

senses.d: Of the same interest or concern; indifferent.
q: They who are not disposed to receive them may let them alone or reject them; it is equal to me.

senses.d: Intended for voices of one kind only, either all male or all female; — opposed to mixed.
Exactly agreeing with respect to quantity.

Equal.syn: Even; equable; uniform; adequate; proportionate; commensurate; fair; just; equitable.
Equal.etym: [L. aequalis, fr. aequus even, equal; akin to Skr. �ka, and perh. to L. unus for older oinos one, E. one.]

senses.d: One not inferior or superior to another; one having the same or a similar age, rank, station, office, talents, strength, or other quality or condition; an equal quantity or number; as, “If equals be taken from equals the remainders are equal.”
q: Those who were once his equals envy and defame him.

senses.d: State of being equal; equality.
To be or become equal to; to have the same quantity, the same value, the same degree or rank, or the like, with; to be commen�urate with.
q: On me whose all not equals Edward's moiety.

senses.d: To make equal return to; to recompense fully.
q: Who answered all her cares, and equaled all her love.

senses.d: To make equal or equal to; to equalize; hence, to compare or regard as equals; to put on equality.
q: He would not equal the mind that he found in himself to the infinite and incomprehensible.

senses.d: The condition or quality of being equal; agreement in quantity or degree as compared; likeness in bulk, value, rank, properties, etc.; as, the equality of two bodies in length or thickness; an equality of rights.
q: A footing of equality with nobles.

senses.d: Sameness in state or continued course; evenness; uniformity; as, an equality of temper or constitution.
Evenness; uniformity; as, an equality of surface.

Exact agreement between two expressions or magnitudes with respect to quantity; — denoted by the symbol =; thus, a = x signifies that a contains the same number and kind of units of measure that x does.

Equality.etym: [L. aequalitas, fr. aequalis equal. See Equal.]

senses.d: In an equal manner or degree in equal shares or proportion; with equal and impartial justice; without difference; alike; evenly; justly; as, equally taxed, furnished, etc.

Equality of rights; natural justice or right; the giving, or desiring to give, to each man his due, according to reason, and the law of God to man; fairness in determination of conflicting claims; impartiality.
q: Christianity secures both the private interests of men and the public peace, enforcing all justice and equity.

senses.d: An equitable claim; an equity of redemption; as, an equity to a settlement, or wife's equity, etc.
q: I consider the wife's equity to be too well settled to be shaken.

senses.d: A system of jurisprudence, supplemental to law, properly so called, and complemental of it.
q: Equity had been gradually shaping itself into a refined science which no human faculties could master without long and intense application.

Equity.syn: Right; justice; impartiality; rectitude; fairness; honesty; uprightness. See Justice.
Equity.etym: [F. équité, L. aequitas, fr. aequus even, equal. See Equal.]

senses.d: Before; sooner than.
q: Myself was stirring ere the break of day.
Ere sails were spread new oceans to explore.
Sir, come down ere my child die.

senses.d: Rather than.
q: I will be thrown into Etna, . . . ere I will leave her.

Ere.etym: [AS. ǣr, prep., adv., & conj.; akin to OS., OFries., & OHG. ēr, G. eher, D. eer, Icel. ār, Goth. air. √204. Cf. Early, Erst, Or, adv.]

senses.d: To plow. See Ear, v. t.
Upright, or having a vertical position; not inverted; not leaning or bent; not prone; as, to stand erect.
q: Two of far nobler shape, erect and tall.
Among the Greek colonies and churches of Asia, Philadelphia is still erect — a column of ruins.

senses.d: Directed upward; raised; uplifted.
q: His piercing eyes, erect, appear to view Superior worlds, and look all nature through.

senses.d: Bold; confident; free from depression; undismayed.
q: But who is he, by years Bowed, but erect in heart?

senses.d: Watchful; alert.
q: Vigilant and erect attention of mind.

senses.d: Standing upright, with reference to the earth's surface, or to the surface to which it is attached.
Elevated, as the tips of wings, heads of serpents, etc.

Erect.etym: [L. erectus, p. p. of erigere to erect; e out + regere to lead straight. See Right, and cf. Alert.]

senses.d: To raise and place in an upright or perpendicular position; to set upright; to raise; as, to erect a pole, a flagstaff, a monument, etc.
To raise, as a building; to build; to construct; as, to erect a house or a fort; to set up; to put together the component parts of, as of a machine.
To lift up; to elevate; to exalt; to magnify.
q: That didst his state above his hopes erect.
I, who am a party, am not to erect myself into a judge.

senses.d: To animate; to encourage; to cheer.
q: It raiseth the dropping spirit, erecting it to a loving complaisance.

senses.d: To set up as an assertion or consequence from premises, or the like.
To set up or establish; to found; to form; to institute.

Erect.syn: To set up; raise; elevate; construct; build; institute; establish; found.

senses.d: To rise upright.
q: By wet, stalks do erect.

senses.d: To wander; to roam; to stray.
q: What seemeth to you, if there were to a man an hundred sheep and one of them hath erred.

senses.d: To deviate from the true course; to miss the thing aimed at.
To miss intellectual truth; to fall into error; to mistake in judgment or opinion; to be mistaken.
q: The man may err in his judgment of circumstances.

senses.d: To deviate morally from the right way; to go astray, in a figurative sense; to do wrong; to sin.
q: Do they not err that devise evil?

senses.d: To offend, as by erring.

Err.etym: [F. errer, L. errare; akin to G. irren, OHG. irran, v. t., irr�n, v. i., OS. irrien, Sw. irra, Dan. irre, Goth, aírzjan to lead astray, airzise astray.]

senses.d: A special business intrusted to a messenger; something to be told or done by one sent somewhere for the purpose; often, a verbal message; a commission; as, the servant was sent on an errand; to do an errand. Also, one's purpose in going anywhere.
q: I have a secret errand to thee, O king.
I will not eat till I have told mine errand.

Errand.etym: [OE. erende, erande, message, business, AS. ærende, ærend; akin to OS. arundi, OHG. arunti, Icel. eyrendi, örendi, erendi, Sw. ärende, Dan. ærende; perh. akin to AS. earu swift, Icel. örr, and to L. oriri to rise, E. orient.]

senses.d: A wandering; a roving or irregular course.
q: The rest of his journey, his error by sea.

senses.d: A wandering or deviation from the right course or standard; irregularity; mistake; inaccuracy; something made wrong or left wrong; as, an error in writing or in printing; a clerical error.
A departing or deviation from the truth; falsity; false notion; wrong opinion; mistake; misapprehension.
q: H� judgment was often in error, though his candor remained unimpaired.

senses.d: A moral offense; violation of duty; a sin or transgression; iniquity; fault.
The difference between the approximate result and the true result; — used particularly in the rule of double position.
The difference between an observed value and the true value of a quantity.
A mistake in the proceedings of a court of record in matters of law or of fact.
A fault of a player of the side in the field which results in failure to put out a player on the other side, or gives him an unearned base.

Error.syn: Mistake; fault; blunder; failure; fallacy; delusion; hallucination; sin. See Blunder.
Error.etym: [OF. error, errur, F. erreur, L. error, fr. errare to err. See Err.]

senses.d: To flee from and avoid; to be saved or exempt from; to shun; to obtain security from; as, to escape danger.
To avoid the notice of; to pass unobserved by; to evade; as, the fact escaped our attention.
q: They escaped the search of the enemy.

Escape.etym: [OE. escapen, eschapen, OF. escaper, eschaper, F. echapper, fr. LL. ex cappa out of one's cape or cloak; hence, to slip out of one's cape and escape. See 3d Cape, and cf. Scape, v.]

senses.d: To flee, and become secure from danger; — often followed by from or out of.
q: Haste, for thy life escape, nor look behind��

senses.d: To get clear from danger or evil of any form; to be passed without harm.
q: Such heretics . . . would have been thought fortunate, if they escaped with life.

senses.d: To get free from that which confines or holds; — used of persons or things; as, to escape from prison, from arrest, or from slavery; gas escapes from the pipes; electricity escapes from its conductors.
q: To escape out of these meshes.

senses.d: The act of fleeing from danger, of evading harm, or of avoiding notice; deliverance from injury or any evil; flight; as, an escape in battle; a narrow escape; also, the means of escape; as, a fire escape.
q: I would hasten my escape from the windy storm.

senses.d: That which escapes attention or restraint; a mistake; an oversight; also, transgression.
q: I should have been more accurate, and corrected all those former escapes.

senses.d: A sally.
The unlawful permission, by a jailer or other custodian, of a prisoner's departure from custody.
An apophyge.
Leakage or outflow, as of steam or a liquid.
Leakage or loss of currents from the conducting wires, caused by defective insulation.
A plant which has escaped from cultivation.
To shun; to avoid, as something wrong, or from a feeling of distaste; to keep one's self clear of.
q: They must not only eschew evil, but do good.

senses.d: To escape from; to avoid.
q: He who obeys, destruction shall eschew.

Eschew.etym: [OF. eschever, eschiver, eskiver, F. esquiver, fr. OHG. sciuhen, G. scheuen; akin to E. sky. See Shy, a.]

senses.d: Distinguished among others of the same class or kind; special; concerning a species or a single object; principal; particular; as, in an especial manner or degree.

Especial.syn: Peculiar; special; particular; uncommon; chief. See Peculiar.
Especial.etym: [OF. especial, F. spécial, L. specialis, fr. species a particular sort, kind, or quality. See Species, and cf. Special.]

senses.d: In an especial manner; chiefly; particularly; peculiarly; in an uncommon degree.
The act of espousing or betrothing; especially, in the plural, betrothal; plighting of the troths; a contract of marriage; sometimes, the marriage ceremony.
The uniting or allying one's self with anything; maintenance; adoption; as, the espousal of a quarrel.
q: The open espousal of his cause.

Espousal.etym: [OF. espousailles, pl., F. épousailles, L. sponsalia, fr. sponsalis belonging to betrothal or espousal. See Espouse, and cf. Sponsal, Spousal.]

senses.d: To betroth; to promise in marriage; to give as spouse.
q: A virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph.

senses.d: To take as spouse; to take to wife; to marry.
q: Lavinia will I make my empress, . . . And in the sacred Pantheon her espouse.

senses.d: To take to one's self with a view to maintain; to make one's own; to take up the cause of; to adopt; to embrace.
q: Promised faithfully to espouse his cause as soon as he got out of the war.

Espouse.etym: [OF. espouser, esposer, F. épouser, L. sponsare to betroth, espouse, fr. sponsus betrothed, p. p. of spondere to promise solemnly or sacredly. Cf. Spouse.]

senses.d: To catch sight of; to perceive with the eyes; to discover, as a distant object partly concealed, or not obvious to notice; to see at a glance; to discern unexpectedly; to spy; as, to espy land; to espy a man in a crowd.
q: As one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, . . . he espied his money.
A goodly vessel did I then espy Come like a giant from a haven broad.

senses.d: To inspect narrowly; to examine and keep watch upon; to watch; to observe.
q: He sends angels to espy us in all our ways.

Espy.syn: To discern; discover; detect; descry; spy.
Espy.etym: [OF. espier, F. épier, from OHG. speh�n to watch, spy, G. spähen; akin to L. specere to look, species sight, shape, appearance, kind. See Spice, Spy, and cf. Espionage.]

senses.d: To look or search narrowly; to look about; to watch; to take notice; to spy.
q: Stand by the way, and espy.

senses.d: A spy; a scout.
To make stable or firm; to fix immovably or firmly; to set (a thing) in a place and make it stable there; to settle; to confirm.
q: So were the churches established in the faith.
The best established tempers can scarcely forbear being borne down.
Confidence which must precede union could be established only by consummate prudence and self-control.

senses.d: To appoint or constitute for permanence, as officers, laws, regulations, etc.; to enact; to ordain.
q: By the consent of all, we were established The people's magistrates.
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed.

senses.d: To originate and secure the permanent existence of; to found; to institute; to create and regulate; — said of a colony, a state, or other institutions.
q: He hath established it , he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited.
Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and establisheth a city by iniquity!

senses.d: To secure public recognition in favor of; to prove and cause to be accepted as true; as, to establish a fact, usage, principle, opinion, doctrine, etc.
q: At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.

senses.d: To set up in business; to place advantageously in a fixed condition; — used reflexively; as, he established himself in a place; the enemy established themselves in the citadel.

Establish.etym: [OE. establissen, OF. establir, F. établir, fr. L. stabilire, fr. stabilis firm, steady, stable. See Stable, a., -ish, and cf. Stablish.]

senses.d: The act of establishing; a ratifying or ordaining; settlement; confirmation.
The state of being established, founded, and the like; fixed state.

That which is established; as: (a) A form of government, civil or ecclesiastical; especially, a system of religion maintained by the civil power; as, the Episcopal establishment of England. (b) A permanent civil, military, or commercial, force or organization. (c) The place in which one is permanently fixed for residence or business; residence, including grounds, furniture, equipage, etc.; with which one is fitted out; also, any office or place of business, with its fixtures; that which serves for the carrying on of a business; as, to keep up a large establishment; a manufacturing establishment.
q: Exposing the shabby parts of the establishment.

senses.d: Settled condition or form of existence; state; condition or circumstances of life or of any person; situation.
q: Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate.

senses.d: Social standing or rank; quality; dignity.
q: God hath imprinted his authority in several parts, upon several estates of men.

senses.d: A person of high rank.
q: She's a duchess, a great estate.
Herod on his birthday made a supper to his lords, high captains, and chief estates of Galilee.

senses.d: A property which a person possesses; a fortune; possessions, esp. property in land; also, property of all kinds which a person leaves to be divided at his death.
q: See what a vast estate he left his son.

senses.d: The state; the general body politic; the common-wealth; the general interest; state affairs.
q: I call matters of estate not only the parts of sovereignty, but whatsoever . . . concerneth manifestly any great portion of people.

senses.d: The great classes or orders of a community or state (as the clergy, the nobility, and the commonalty of England) or their representatives who administer the government; as, the estates of the realm (England), which are (1) the lords spiritual, (2) the lords temporal, (3) the commons.
The degree, quality, nature, and extent of one's interest in, or ownership of, lands, tenements, etc.; as, an estate for life, for years, at will, etc.

Estate.etym: [OF. estat, F. état, L. status, fr. stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. State.]

senses.d: To establish.
Tom settle as a fortune.
To endow with an estate.
q: Then would I . . . Estate them with large land and territory.

senses.d: To set a value on; to appreciate the worth of; to estimate; to value; to reckon.
q: Then he forsook God, which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.
Thou shouldst (gentle reader) esteem his censure and authority to be of the more weighty credence.
Famous men, — whose scientific attainments were esteemed hardly less than supernatural.

senses.d: To set a high value on; to prize; to regard with reverence, respect, or friendship.
q: Will he esteem thy riches?
You talk kindlier: we esteem you for it.

Esteem.syn: To estimate; appreciate; regard; prize; value; respect; revere. See Appreciate, Estimate.
Esteem.etym: [F. estimer, L. aestimare, aestumare, to value, estimate; perh. akin to Skr. ish to seek, strive, and E. ask. Cf. Aim, Estimate.]

senses.d: To form an estimate; to have regard to the value; to consider.
q: We ourselves esteem not of that obedience, or love, or gift, which is of force.

senses.d: Estimation; opinion of merit or value; hence, valuation; reckoning; price.
q: Most dear in the esteem And poor in worth!
I will deliver you, in ready coin, The full and dear'st esteem of what you crave.

senses.d: High estimation or value; great regard; favorable opinion, founded on supposed worth.
q: Nor should thy prowess want praise and esteem.

Esteem.etym: [Cf. F. estime. See Esteem, v. t.]

senses.d: To judge and form an opinion of the value of, from imperfect data, — either the extrinsic (money), or intrinsic (moral), value; to fix the worth of roughly or in a general way; as, to estimate the value of goods or land; to estimate the worth or talents of a person.
q: It is by the weight of silver, and not the name of the piece, that men estimate commodities and exchange them.
It is always very difficult to estimate the age in which you are living.

senses.d: To from an opinion of, as to amount,, number, etc., from imperfect data, comparison, or experience; to make an estimate of; to calculate roughly; to rate; as, to estimate the cost of a trip, the number of feet in a piece of land.

Estimate.syn: To appreciate; value; appraise; prize; rate; esteem; count; calculate; number. — To Estimate, Esteem. Both these words imply an exercise of the judgment. Estimate has reference especially to the external relations of things, such as amount, magnitude, importance, etc. It usually involves computation or calculation; as, to estimate the loss or gain of an enterprise. Esteem has reference to the intrinsic or moral worth of a person or thing. Thus, we esteem a man for his kindness, or his uniform integrity. In this sense it implies a mingled sentiment of respect and attachment. We esteem it an hon
Estimate.etym: [L. aestimatus, p. p. of aestimare. See Esteem, v. t.]

senses.d: A valuing or rating by the mind, without actually measuring, weighing, or the like; rough or approximate calculation; as, an estimate of the cost of a building, or of the quantity of water in a pond.
q: Weigh success in a moral balance, and our whole estimate is changed.

senses.d: The act of estimating.
An opinion or judgment of the worth, extent, or quantity of anything, formed without using precise data; valuation; as, estimations of distance, magnitude, amount, or moral qualities.
q: If he be poorer that thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest, and the priest shall value him.

senses.d: Favorable opinion; esteem; regard; honor.
q: I shall have estimation among multitude, and honor with the elders.

senses.d: Supposition; conjecture.
q: I speak not this in estimation, As what I think might be, but what I know.

Estimation.syn: Estimate; calculation; computation; appraisement; esteem; honor; regard. See Estimate, n.
Estimation.etym: [L. aestimatio, fr. aestimare: cf. F. estimation. See Esteem, v. t.]

senses.d: To withdraw; to withhold; hence, reflexively, to keep at a distance; to cease to be familiar and friendly with.
q: We must estrange our belief from everything which is not clearly and distinctly evidenced.
Had we . . . estranged ourselves from them in things indifferent.

senses.d: To divert from its original use or purpose, or from its former possessor; to alienate.
q: They . . . have estranged this place, and have burned incense in it unto other gods.

senses.d: To alienate the affections or confidence of; to turn from attachment to enmity or indifference.
q: I do not know, to this hour, what it is that has estranged him from me.
He . . . had pretended to be estranged from the Whigs, and had promised to act as a spy upon them.

Estrange.etym: [OF. estrangier to remove, F. étranger, L. extraneare to treat as a stranger, from extraneus strange. See Strange.]

senses.d: Without beginning or end of existence; always existing.
q: The eternal God is thy refuge.
To know wether there were any real being, whose duration has been eternal.

senses.d: Without end of existence or duration; everlasting; endless; immortal.
q: That they may also obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory.

senses.d: Continued without intermission; perpetual; ceaseless; constant.
q: And fires eternal in thy temple shine.

senses.d: Existing at all times without change; immutable.
q: Hobbes believed the eternal truths which he opposed.
What are the eternal objects of poetry among all nations, and at all times?

senses.d: Exceedingly great or bad; — used as a strong intensive.

Eternal.syn: Everlasting; endless; infinite; ceaseless; perpetual; interminable. See Everlasting.
Eternal.etym: [F. éternel, L. aeternalis, fr. aeternus. See Etern.]

senses.d: One of the appellations of God.
q: Law whereby the Eternal himself doth work.

senses.d: That which is endless and immortal.
Infinite duration, without beginning in the past or end in the future; also, duration without end in the future; endless time.
q: The high and lofty One, that inhabiteth eternity.

senses.d: Condition which begins at death; immortality.
q: Thou know'st 't is common; all that lives must die, Passing through nature to eternity.

Eternity.etym: [F. éternité, L. aeternitas, fr. aeternus. See Etern.]

senses.d: Easy.

A medium of great elasticity and extreme tenuity, supposed to pervade all space, the interior of solid bodies not excepted, and to be the medium of transmission of light and heat; hence often called luminiferous ether.
Supposed matter above the air; the air itself.

A light, volatile, mobile, inflammable liquid, (C2H5)2O, of a characteristic aromatic odor, obtained by the distillation of alcohol with sulphuric acid, and hence called also sulphuric ether. It is powerful solvent of fats, resins, and pyroxylin, but finds its chief use as an anæsthetic. Called also ethyl oxide.

Ether.etym: [L. aether, Gr. αιθἤρ, fr. αἴθειν to light up, kindle, burn, blaze; akin to Skr. idh, indh, and prob. to E. idle: cf. F. éther.]

senses.d: Of or relating to Ethiopia or the Ethiopians.

A male of the human species castrated; commonly, one of a class of such persons, in Oriental countries, having charge of the women's apartments. Some of them, in former times, gained high official rank.

Eunuch.etym: [L. eunuchus, Gr. �, prop., keeping or guarding the couch; � couch, bed, + � to have, hold, keep.]

senses.d: To make a eunuch of; to castrate. as a man.
A tempestuous northeast wind which blows in the Mediterranean. See Levanter.
q: A tempestuous wind called Euroclydon.

Euroclydon.etym: [NL., fr. Gr. �; � the southeast wind + � wave, billow; according to another reading, �, i.e. a north-east wind, as in the Latin Vulgate Euro-aquilo.]

senses.d: A bringer of the glad tidings of Church and his doctrines.
A missionary preacher sent forth to prepare the way for a resident pastor; an itinerant missionary preacher.
A writer of one of the four Gospels (With the definite article); as, the four evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
A traveling preacher whose efforts are chiefly directed to arouse to immediate repentance.
q: The Apostles, so far as they evangelized, might claim the title though there were many evangelists who were not Apostles.

Evangelist.etym: [F. évangéliste, L. evangelista, fr. Gr. ευαγγελιστἤσ.]

senses.d: Evangel.
q: The sacred pledge of Christ's evangely.

senses.d: Evening.
q: Winter oft, at eve resumes the breeze.

senses.d: The evening before a holiday, — from the Jewish mode of reckoning the day as beginning at sunset, not at midnight; as, Christmas eve is the evening before Christmas; also, the period immediately preceding some important event.
Evening. See Eve, n. 1.

Even.etym: [OE. eve, even, efen, æfen. AS. ǣfen; akin to OS. āband, OFries, āvend, D. avond, OHG. āband, Icel. aptan, Sw. afton, Dan. aften; of unknown origin. Cf. Eve, Evening.]

senses.d: Level, smooth, or equal in surface; not rough; free from irregularities; hence uniform in rate of motion of action; as, even ground; an even speed; an even course of conduct.
Equable; not easily ruffled or disturbed; calm; uniformly self-possessed; as, an even temper.
Parallel; on a level; reaching the same limit.
q: And shall lay thee even with the ground.

senses.d: Balanced; adjusted; fair; equitable; impartial; just to both sides; owing nothing on either side; — said of accounts, bargains, or persons indebted; as, our accounts are even; an even bargain.
q: To make the even truth in pleasure flow.

senses.d: Without an irregularity, flaw, or blemish; pure.
Associate; fellow; of the same condition.
Not odd; capable of division by two without a remainder; — said of numbers; as, 4 and 10 are even numbers.
q: Whether the number of the stars is even or odd.

Even.etym: [AS. efen. efn; akin to OS. eban, D. even, OHG. eban, G. efen, Icel. jafn, Dan. jevn, Sw. jämn, Goth. ibns. Cf. Anent, Ebb.]

senses.d: To make even or level; to level; to lay smooth.
q: His temple Xerxes evened with the soil.
It will even all inequalities

senses.d: To equal.
To place in an equal state, as to obligation, or in a state in which nothing is due on either side; to balance, as accounts; to make quits.
To set right; to complete.
To act up to; to keep pace with.
To be equal.
In an equal or precisely similar manner; equally; precisely; just; likewise; as well.
q: Even so did these Gauls possess the coast.

senses.d: Up to, or down to, an unusual measure or level; so much as; fully; quite.
q: Thou wast a soldier Even to Cato's wish.
Without . . . making us even sensible of the change.

senses.d: As might not be expected; — serving to introduce what is unexpected or less expected.
q: I have made several discoveries, which appear new, even to those who are versed in critical learning.

senses.d: At the very time; in the very case.
q: I knew they were bad enough to please, even when I wrote them.
By these presence, even the presence of Lord Mortimer.

Even.etym: [AS. efne. See Even, a., and cf. E'en.]

senses.d: To happen.
The latter part and close of the day, and the beginning of darkness or night; properly, the decline of the day, or of the sun.
q: In the ascending scale Of heaven, the stars that usher evening rose.

senses.d: The latter portion, as of life; the declining period, as of strength or glory.

Evening.etym: [AS. ǣfnung. See even, n., and cf. Eve.]

senses.d: That which comes, arrives, or happens; that which falls out; any incident, good or bad.
q: To watch quietly the course of events.
There is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked.

senses.d: An affair in hand; business; enterprise.
The consequence of anything; the issue; conclusion; result; that in which an action, operation, or series of operations, terminates.
q: Dark doubts between the promise and event.

Event.syn: Incident; occurrence; adventure; issue; result; termination; consequence; conclusion.
Event.etym: [L. eventus, fr. evenire to happen, come out; e out + venire to come. See Come.]

senses.d: To break forth.

Event.etym: [F. éventer to fan, divulge, LL. eventare to fan, fr., L. e out + ventus wind.]

senses.d: The time of evening; evening.
At any time; at any period or point of time.
q: No man ever yet hated his own flesh.

senses.d: At all times; through all time; always; forever.
q: He shall ever love, and always be The subject of by scorn and cruelty.

senses.d: Without cessation; continually.
q: To produce as much as ever they can.

Ever.etym: [OE. ever, æfre, AS. æfre; perh. akin to AS. ā always. Cf. Aye, Age,Evry, Never.]

senses.d: Lasting or enduring forever; exsisting or continuing without end; immortal; eternal.
Continuing indefinitely, or during a long period; perpetual; sometimes used, colloquially, as a strong intensive; as, this everlasting nonsence.
q: I will give to thee, and to thy seed after thee . . . the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession.
And heard thy everlasting yawn confess The pains and penalties of idleness.
Whether we shall meet again I know not; Therefore our everlasting farewell take; Forever, and forever farewell, Cassius.

Everlasting.syn: Eternal; immortal, interminable; endless; never-ending; infinite; unceasing; uninterrupted; continual; unintermitted; incessant.

senses.d: Eternal duration, past or future; eternity.
q: From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

senses.d: (With the definite article) The Eternal Being; God.
A plant whose flowers may be dried without losing their form or color, as the pearly everlasting (Anaphalis margaritacea), the immortelle of the French, the cudweeds, etc.
A cloth fabric for shoes, etc. See Lasting.
During eternity; always; forever; for an indefinite period; at all times; — often used substantively with for.
q: Seek the Lord . . . Seek his face evermore.
And, behold, I am alive for evermore.
Which flow from the presence of God for evermore.
I evermore did love you, Hermia.

senses.d: All the parts which compose a whole collection or aggregate number, considered in their individuality, all taken separately one by one, out of an indefinite number.
q: Every man at his best state is altogether vanity.
Every door and window was adorned with wreaths of flowers.

senses.d: Every one. Cf. Each.
q: Daily occasions given to every of us.
In each division there were four pentecosties, in every pentecosty four enomoties, and of each enomoty there fought in the front rank four .
If society is to be kept together and the children of Adam to be saved from setting up each for himself with every one else his foe.

Every.etym: [OE. everich, everilk; AS. ǣfre ever + ælc each. See Ever, each.]

senses.d: That which makes evident or manifest; that which furnishes, or tends to furnish, proof; any mode of proof; the ground of belief or judgement; as, the evidence of our senses; evidence of the truth or falsehood of a statement.
q: Faith is . . . the evidence of things not seen.
O glorious trial of exceeding love Illustrious evidence, example high.

senses.d: One who bears witness.

That which is legally submitted to competent tribunal, as a means of ascertaining the truth of any alleged matter of fact under investigation before it; means of making proof; — the latter, strictly speaking, not being synonymous with evidence, but rather the effect of it.
To render evident or clear; to prove; to evince; as, to evidence a fact, or the guilt of an offender.

Clear to the vision; especially, clear to the understanding, and satisfactory to the judgment; as, the figure or color of a body is evident to the senses; the guilt of an offender can not always be made evident.
q: Your honor and your goodness is so evident.
And in our faces evident the signs Of foul concupiscence.

Evident.syn: Manifest; plain; clear; obvious; visible; apparent; conclusive; indubitable; palpable; notorious. See Manifest.
Evident.etym: [F. évinent, l. evidens, -entis; e out + videns, p. pr. of videre to see. See Vision.]

senses.d: In an evident manner; clearly; plainly.
q: Before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth.
He was evidently in the prime of youth.

senses.d: Having qualities tending to injury and mischief; having a nature or properties which tend to badness; mischievous; not good; worthless or deleterious; poor; as, an evil beast; and evil plant; an evil crop.
q: A good tree can not bring forth evil fruit.

senses.d: Having or exhibiting bad moral qualities; morally corrupt; wicked; wrong; vicious; as, evil conduct, thoughts, heart, words, and the like.
q: Ah, what a sign it is of evil life, When death's approach is seen so terrible.

senses.d: Producing or threatening sorrow, distress, injury, or calamity; unpropitious; calamitous; as, evil tidings; evil arrows; evil days.
q: Because he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel.
The owl shrieked at thy birth — an evil sign.
Evil news rides post, while good news baits.

Evil.syn: Mischieveous; pernicious; injurious; hurtful; destructive; wicked; sinful; bad; corrupt; perverse; wrong; vicious; calamitous.
Evil.etym: [OE. evel, evil, ifel, uvel, AS. yfel; akin to OFries, evel, D. euvel, OS. & OHG. ubil, G. übel, Goth. ubils, and perh. to E. over.]

senses.d: Anything which impairs the happiness of a being or deprives a being of any good; anything which causes suffering of any kind to sentient beings; injury; mischief; harm; — opposed to good.
q: Evils which our own misdeeds have wrought.
The evil that men do lives after them.

senses.d: Moral badness, or the deviation of a moral being from the principles of virtue imposed by conscience, or by the will of the Supreme Being, or by the principles of a lawful human authority; disposition to do wrong; moral offence; wickedness; depravity.
q: The heart of the sons of men is full of evil.

senses.d: malady or disease; especially in the phrase king's evil, the scrofula.
q: He was the first that touched for the evil.

senses.d: In an evil manner; not well; ill; badly; unhappily; injuriously; unkindly.
q: It went evil with his house.
The Egyptians evil entreated us, and affected us.

senses.d: A yew.
The female of the sheep, and of sheeplike animals.

Ewe.etym: [AS. eówu; akin to D. ooi, OHG. awi, ouwi, Icel. ær, Goth. awēþi a flock of sheep, awistr a sheepfold, Lith. avis a sheep, L. ovis, Gr. ὄϊσ, Skr. avi. √231.]

senses.d: Precisely agreeing with a standard, a fact, or the truth; perfectly conforming; neither exceeding nor falling short in any respect; true; correct; precise; as, the clock keeps exact time; he paid the exact debt; an exact copy of a letter; exact accounts.
q: I took a great pains to make out the exact truth.

senses.d: Habitually careful to agree with a standard, a rule, or a promise; accurate; methodical; punctual; as, a man exact in observing an appointment; in my doings I was exact.
Precisely or definitely conceived or stated; strict.
q: An exact command, Larded with many several sorts of reason.

Exact.etym: [L. exactus precise, accurate, p. p. of exigere to drive out, to demand, enforce, finish, determine, measure; ex out + agere to drive; cf. F. exact. See Agent, Act.]

senses.d: To demand or require authoritatively or peremptorily, as a right; to enforce the payment of, or a yielding of; to compel to yield or to furnish; hence, to wrest, as a fee or reward when none is due; — followed by from or of before the one subjected to exaction; as, to exact tribute, fees, obedience, etc., from or of some one.
q: He said into them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you.
Years of servise past From grateful souls exact reward at last
My designs Exact me in another place.

Exact.etym: [From L. exactus, p. p. of exigere; or fr. LL. exactare: cf. OF. exacter. See Exact, a.]

senses.d: To practice exaction.
q: The anemy shall not exact upon him.

senses.d: The act of demanding with authority, and compelling to pay or yield; compulsion to give or furnish; a levying by force; a driving to compliance; as, the exaction to tribute or of obedience; hence, extortion.
q: Take away your exactions from my people.
Daily new exactions are devised.
Illegal exactions of sheriffs and officials.

senses.d: That which is exacted; a severe tribute; a fee, reward, or contribution, demanded or levied with severity or injustice.
One who exacts or demands by authority or right; hence, an extortioner; also, one unreasonably severe in injunctions or demands.
To raise high; to elevate; to lift up.
q: I will exalt my throne above the stars of God.
Exalt thy towery head, and lift thine eyes

senses.d: To elevate in rank, dignity, power, wealth, character, or the like; to dignify; to promote; as, to exalt a prince to the throne, a citizen to the presidency.
q: Righteousness exalteth a nation.
He that humbleth himself shall be exalted.

senses.d: To elevate by prise or estimation; to magnify; to extol; to glorify.
q: In his own grace he doth exalt himself.

senses.d: To lift up with joy, pride, or success; to inspire with delight or satisfaction; to elate.
q: They who thought they got whatsoever he lost were mightily exalted.

senses.d: To elevate the tone of, as of the voice or a musical instrument.
q: Now Mars, she said, let Fame exalt her voice.

senses.d: To render pure or refined; to intensify or concentrate; as, to exalt the juices of bodies.
q: With chemic art exalts the mineral powers.

Exalt.etym: [L. exaltare; ex out (intens.) + altare to make high, altus high: cf.F. exalter. See Altitude.]

senses.d: Raised to lofty height; elevated; extolled; refined; dignified; sublime.
q: Wiser far than Solomon, Of more exalted mind.
Time never fails to bring every exalted reputation to a strict scrutiny.

senses.d: The act of examining, or state of being examined; a careful search, investigation, or inquiry; scrutiny by study or experiment.
A process prescribed or assigned for testing qualification; as, the examination of a student, or of a candidate for admission to the bar or the ministry.
q: He neglected the studies, . . . stood low at the examinations.

Examination.syn: Search; inquiry; investigation; research; scrutiny; inquisition; inspection; exploration.

senses.d: To test by any appropriate method; to inspect carefully with a view to discover the real character or state of; to subject to inquiry or inspection of particulars for the purpose of obtaining a fuller insight into the subject of examination, as a material substance, a fact, a reason, a cause, the truth of a statement; to inquire or search into; to explore; as, to examine a mineral; to examine a ship to know whether she is seaworthy; to examine a proposition, theory, or question.
q: Examine well your own thoughts.
Examine their counsels and their cares.

senses.d: To interrogate as in a judicial proceeding; to try or test by question; as, to examine a witness in order to elicit testimony, a student to test his qualifications, a bankrupt touching the state of his property, etc.
q: The offenders that are to be examined.

Examine.syn: To discuss; debate; scrutinize; search into; investigate; explore. See Discuss.
Examine.etym: [L. examinare, examinatum, fr. examen, examinis: cf. F. examiner. See Examen.]

senses.d: Having power to examine; appointed to examine; as, an examining committee.
One or a portion taken to show the character or quality of the whole; a sample; a specimen.
That which is to be followed or imitated as a model; a pattern or copy.
q: For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
I gave, thou sayest, the example; I led the way.

senses.d: That which resembles or corresponds with something else; a precedent; a model.
q: Such temperate order in so fierce a cause Doth want example.

senses.d: That which is to be avoided; one selected for punishment and to serve as a warning; a warning.
q: Hang him; he'll be made an example.
Now these things were our examples, to the intent that we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.

senses.d: An instance serving for illustration of a rule or precept, especially a problem to be solved, or a case to be determined, as an exercise in the application of the rules of any study or branch of science; as, in trigonometry and grammar, the principles and rules are illustrated by examples.

Example.etym: [A later form for ensample, fr. L. exemplum, orig., what is taken out of a larger quantity, as a sample, from eximere to take out. See Exempt, and cf. Ensample, Sample.]

senses.d: To set an example for; to give a precedent for; to exemplify; to give an instance of; to instance.
q: Burke devoted himself to this duty with a fervid assiduity that has not often been exampled, and has never been surpassed.

senses.d: To go beyond; to proceed beyond the given or supposed limit or measure of; to outgo; to surpass; — used both in a good and a bad sense; as, one man exceeds another in bulk, stature, weight, power, skill, etc.; one offender exceeds another in villainy; his rank exceeds yours.
q: Name the time, but let it not Exceed three days.
Observes how much a chintz exceeds mohair.

Exceed.syn: To outdo; surpass; excel; transcend; outstrip; outvie; overtop.
Exceed.etym: [L. excedere, excessum, to go away or beyond; ex out + cedere to go, to pass: cf. F. excéder. See Cede.]

senses.d: To go too far; to pass the proper bounds or measure.
q: Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed.

senses.d: To be more or greater; to be paramount.
More than usual; extraordinary; more than sufficient; measureless.
In a very great degree; extremely; exceedingly.
q: His raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow.
The Genoese were exceeding powerful by sea.

senses.d: To a very great degree; beyond what is usual; surpassingly. It signifies more than very.
To go beyond or surpass in good qualities or laudable deeds; to outdo or outgo, in a good sense.
q: Excelling others, these were great; Thou, greater still, must these excel.
I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.

senses.d: To exceed or go beyond; to surpass.
q: She opened; but to shut Excelled her power; the gates wide open stood.

Excel.etym: [L. excellere, excelsum; ex out + a root found in culmen height, top; cf. F. exceller. See Culminate, Column.]

senses.d: To surpass others in good qualities, laudable actions, or acquirements; to be distinguished by superiority; as, to excel in mathematics, or classics.
q: Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel.
Then peers grew proud in horsemanship t' excel.

senses.d: Excellence; virtue; dignity; worth; superiority.
q: His excellency is over Israel.
Extinguish in men the sense of their own excellency.

senses.d: A title of honor given to certain high dignitaries, esp. to viceroys, ministers, and ambassadors, to English colonial governors, etc. It was formerly sometimes given to kings and princes.

Excelling; surpassing others in some good quality or the sum of qualities; of great worth; eminent, in a good sense; superior; as, an excellent man, artist, citizen, husband, discourse, book, song, etc.; excellent breeding, principles, aims, action.
q: To love . . . What I see excellent in good or fair.

senses.d: Superior in kind or degree, irrespective of moral quality; — used with words of a bad significance.
q: Their sorrows are most excellent.

Excellent.syn: Worthy; choice; prime; valuable; select; exquisite; transcendent; admirable; worthy.
Excellent.etym: [F. excellent, L. excellens, -entis, p. pr. of excellere. See Excel.]

senses.d: Excellently; eminently; exceedingly.
To take or leave out (anything) from a number or a whole as not belonging to it; to exclude; to omit.
q: Who never touched The excepted tree.
Wherein (if we only except the unfitness of the judge) all other things concurred.

senses.d: To object to; to protest against.

Except.etym: [L. exceptus, p. p. of excipere to take or draw out, to except; ex out + capere to take: cf. F. excepter. See Capable.]

senses.d: To take exception; to object; — usually followed by to, sometimes by against; as, to except to a witness or his testimony.
q: Except thou wilt except against my love.

senses.d: With exclusion of; leaving or left out; excepting.
q: God and his Son except, Created thing naught valued he nor . . . shunned.

senses.d: Unless; if it be not so that.
q: And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
But yesterday you never opened lip, Except, indeed, to drink.

senses.d: The state of surpassing or going beyond limits; the being of a measure beyond sufficiency, necessity, or duty; that which exceeds what is usual or proper; immoderateness; superfluity; superabundance; extravagance; as, an excess of provisions or of light.
q: To gild refined gold, to paint the lily, To throw a perfume on the violet, . . . Is wasteful and ridiculous excess.
That kills me with excess of grief, this with excess of joy.

senses.d: An undue indulgence of the appetite; transgression of proper moderation in natural gratifications; intemperance; dissipation.
q: Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess.
Thy desire . . . leads to no excess That reaches blame.

senses.d: The degree or amount by which one thing or number exceeds another; remainder; as, the difference between two numbers is the excess of one over the other.

Excess.etym: [OE. exces, excess, ecstasy, L. excessus a going out, loss of self-possession, fr. excedere, excessum, to go out, go beyond: cf. F. excès. See Exceed.]

senses.d: The act of giving or taking one thing in return for another which is regarded as an equivalent; as, an exchange of cattle for grain.

The act of substituting one thing in the place of another; as, an exchange of grief for joy, or of a scepter for a sword, and the like; also, the act of giving and receiving reciprocally; as, an exchange of civilities or views.
The thing given or received in return; esp., a publication exchanged for another.

The process of setting accounts or debts between parties residing at a distance from each other, without the intervention of money, by exchanging orders or drafts, called bills of exchange. These may be drawn in one country and payable in another, in which case they are called foreign bills; or they may be drawn and made payable in the same country, in which case they are called inland bills. The term bill of exchange is often abbreviated into exchange; as, to buy or sell exchange.
A mutual grant of equal interests, the one in consideration of the other. Estates exchanged must be equal in quantity, as fee simple for fee simple.
The place where the merchants, brokers, and bankers of a city meet at certain hours, to transact business. In this sense often contracted to 'Change.

Exchange.etym: [OE. eschange, eschaunge, OF. eschange, fr. eschangier, F. échanger, to exchange; pref. ex- out + F. changer. See Change, and cf. Excamb.]

senses.d: To part with give, or transfer to another in consideration of something received as an equivalent; — usually followed by for before the thing received.
q: Exchange his sheep for shells, or wool for a sparking pebble or a diamond.

senses.d: To part with for a substitute; to lay aside, quit, or resign (something being received in place of the thing parted with); as, to exchange a palace for cell.
q: And death for life exchanged foolishly.
To shift his being Is to exchange one misery with another.

senses.d: To give and receive reciprocally, as things of the same kind; to barter; to swap; as, to exchange horses with a neighbor; to exchange houses or hats.
q: Exchange forgiveness with me, noble Hamlet.

Exchange.syn: To barter; change; commute; interchange; bargain; truck; swap; traffic.
Exchange.etym: [Cf.OF. eschangier, F. échanger. See Exchange, n.]

senses.d: To be changed or received in exchange for; to pass in exchange; as, dollar exchanges for ten dimes.
One who exchanges; one who practices exchange.

To shut out; to hinder from entrance or admission; to debar from participation or enjoyment; to deprive of; to except; — the opposite to admit; as, to exclude a crowd from a room or house; to exclude the light; to exclude one nation from the ports of another; to exclude a taxpayer from the privilege of voting.
q: And none but such, from mercy I exclude.

senses.d: To thrust out or eject; to expel; as, to exclude young animals from the womb or from eggs.

Exclude.etym: [L. excludere, exclusum; ex out + claudere to shut. See Close.]

senses.d: To free from accusation, or the imputation of fault or blame; to clear from guilt; to release from a charge; to justify by extenuating a fault; to exculpate; to absolve; to acquit.
q: A man's persuasion that a thing is duty, will not excuse him from guilt in practicing it, if really and indeed it be against Gog's law.

senses.d: To pardon, as a fault; to forgive entirely, or to admit to be little censurable, and to overlook; as, we excuse irregular conduct, when extraordinary circumstances appear to justify it.
q: I must excuse what can not be amended.

senses.d: To regard with indulgence; to view leniently or to overlook; to pardon.
q: And in our own (excuse some courtly stains.) No whiter page than Addison remains.

senses.d: To free from an impending obligation or duty; hence, to disengage; to dispense with; to release by favor; also, to remit by favor; not to exact; as, to excuse a forfeiture.
q: I pray thee have me excused.

senses.d: To relieve of an imputation by apology or defense; to make apology for as not seriously evil; to ask pardon or indulgence for.
q: Think ye that we excuse ourselves to you?

Excuse.etym: [OE. escusen, cusen, OF. escuser, excuser, F. excuser, fr. L. excusare; ex out + causa cause, causari to plead. See Cause.]

senses.d: The act of excusing, apologizing, exculpating, pardoning, releasing, and the like; acquittal; release; absolution; justification; extenuation.
q: Pleading so wisely in excuse of it.

senses.d: That which is offered as a reason for being excused; a plea offered in extenuation of a fault or irregular deportment; apology; as, an excuse for neglect of duty; excuses for delay of payment.
q: Hence with denial vain and coy excuse.

senses.d: That which excuses; that which extenuates or justifies a fault.
q: If eyes were made for seeing. Then beauty is its own excuse for being.

Excuse.etym: [Cf. F. excuse. See Excuse, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of cursing; a curse dictated by violent feelings of hatred; imprecation; utter detestation expressed.
q: Cease, gentle, queen, these execrations.

senses.d: That which is execrated; a detested thing.
q: Ye shall be an execration and . . . a curse.

senses.d: To follow out or through to the end; to carry out into complete effect; to complete; to finish; to effect; to perform.
q: Why delays His hand to execute what his decree Fixed on this day?

senses.d: To complete, as a legal instrument; to perform what is required to give validity to, as by signing and perhaps sealing and delivering; as, to execute a deed, lease, mortgage, will, etc.
To give effect to; to do what is provided or required by; to perform the requirements or stipulations of; as, to execute a decree, judgment, writ, or process.
To infect capital punishment on; to put to death in conformity to a legal sentence; as, to execute a traitor.
To put to death illegally; to kill.
To perform, as a piece of music, either on an instrument or with the voice; as, to execute a difficult part brilliantly.

Execute.syn: To accomplish; effect; fulfill; achieve; consummate; finish; complete. See Accomplish.
Execute.etym: [F. exécuter, L. executus, exsecutus, p. p. of exequi to follow to the end, pursue; ex out + sequi to follow. See Second, Sue to follow up, and cf. Exequy.]

senses.d: To do one's work; to act one's part or purpose.
To perform musically.
The act of executing; a carrying into effect or to completion; performance; achievement; consummation; as, the execution of a plan, a work, etc.
q: The excellence of the subject contributed much to the happiness of the execution.

senses.d: A putting to death as a legal penalty; death lawfully inflicted; as, the execution of a murderer.
q: A warrant for his execution.

senses.d: The act of the mode of performing a work of art, of performing on an instrument, of engraving, etc.; as, the execution of a statue, painting, or piece of music.
q: The first quality of execution is truth.

senses.d: The carrying into effect the judgment given in a court of law.
That which is executed or accomplished; effect; effective work; — usually with do.
q: To do some fatal execution.

senses.d: The act of sacking a town.
One who executes; an executer.
One who puts to death in conformity to legal warrant, as a hangman.
Cut off; set apart.
q: Corrupted, and exempt from ancient gentry.

senses.d: Extraordinary; exceptional.

Free, or released, from some liability to which others are subject; excepted from the operation or burden of some law; released; free; clear; privileged; — (with from): not subject to; not liable to; as, goods exempt from execution; a person exempt from jury service.
q: True nobility is exempt from fear.
T is laid on all, not any one exempt.

Exempt.etym: [F. exempt, L. exemptus, p. p. of eximere to take out, remove, free; ex out + emere to buy, take. Cf. Exon, Redeem.]

senses.d: One exempted or freed from duty; one not subject.
One of four officers of the Yeomen of the Royal Guard, having the rank of corporal; an Exon.
To remove; to set apart.

To release or deliver from some liability which others are subject to; to except or excuse from he operation of a law; to grant immunity to; to free from obligation; to release; as, to exempt from military duty, or from jury service; to exempt from fear or pain.
q: Death So snatched will not exempt us from the pain We are by doom to pay.

senses.d: The act of exercising; a setting in action or practicing; employment in the proper mode of activity; exertion; application; use; habitual activity; occupation, in general; practice.
q: exercise of the important function confided by the constitution to the legislature.
O we will walk this world, Yoked in all exercise of noble end.

senses.d: Exertion for the sake of training or improvement whether physical, intellectual, or moral; practice to acquire skill, knowledge, virtue, perfectness, grace, etc.
q: An exercise of the eyes and memory.

senses.d: Bodily exertion for the sake of keeping the organs and functions in a healthy state; hygienic activity; as, to take exercise on horseback.
q: The wise for cure on exercise depend.

senses.d: The performance of an office, a ceremony, or a religious duty.
q: Lewis refused even those of the church of England . . . the public exercise of their religion.
To draw him from his holy exercise.

senses.d: That which is done for the sake of exercising, practicing, training, or promoting skill, health, mental, improvement, moral discipline, etc.; that which is assigned or prescribed for such ends; hence, a disquisition; a lesson; a task; as, military or naval exercises; musical exercises; an exercise in composition.
q: The clumsy exercises of the European tourney.
He seems to have taken a degree, and performed public exercises in Cambridge, in 1565.

senses.d: That which gives practice; a trial; a test.
q: Patience is more oft the exercise Of saints, the trial of their fortitude.

Exercise.etym: [F. exercice, L. exercitium, from exercere, exercitum, to drive on, keep, busy, prob. orig., to thrust or drive out of the inclosure; ex out + arcere to shut up, inclose. See Ark.]

senses.d: To set in action; to cause to act, move, or make exertion; to give employment to; to put in action habitually or constantly; to school or train; to exert repeatedly; to busy.
q: Herein do I Exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence.

senses.d: To exert for the sake of training or improvement; to practice in order to develop; hence, also, to improve by practice; to discipline, and to use or to for the purpose of training; as, to exercise arms; to exercise one's self in music; to exercise troops.
q: About him exercised heroic games The unarmed youth.

senses.d: To occupy the attention and effort of; to task; to tax, especially in a painful or vexatious manner; harass; to vex; to worry or make anxious; to affect; to discipline; as, exercised with pain.
q: Where pain of unextinguishable fire Must exercise us without hope of end.

senses.d: To put in practice; to carry out in action; to perform the duties of; to use; to employ; to practice; as, to exercise authority; to exercise an office.
q: I am the Lord which exercise loving-kindness, judgment, and righteousness in the earth.
The people of the land have used oppression and exercised robbery.

senses.d: To exercise one's self, as under military training; to drill; to take exercise; to use action or exertion; to practice gymnastics; as, to exercise for health or amusement.
q: I wear my trusty sword, When I do exercise.

senses.d: To incite by words or advice; to animate or urge by arguments, as to a good deed or laudable conduct; to address exhortation to; to urge strongly; hence, to advise, warn, or caution.
q: Examples gross as earth exhort me.
Let me exhort you to take care of yourself.

Exhort.etym: [L. exhortari; ex out + hortari to incite, encourage; cf. F. exhorter. See Hortative.]

senses.d: To deliver exhortation; to use words or arguments to incite to good deeds.
q: With many other words did he testify and exhort.

senses.d: Exhortation.
The act of practice of exhorting; the act of inciting to laudable deeds; incitement to that which is good or commendable.
Language intended to incite and encourage; advice; counsel; admonition.
q: I'll end my exhortation after dinner.

senses.d: Forced separation from one's native country; expulsion from one's home by the civil authority; banishment; sometimes, voluntary separation from one's native country.
q: Let them be recalled from their exile.

senses.d: The person expelled from his country by authority; also, one who separates himself from his home.
q: Thou art in exile, and thou must not stay.

Exile.etym: [OE. exil, fr. L. exilium, exsilium, fr. exsuil one who quits, or is banished from, his native soil; ex out + solum ground, land, soil, or perh. fr.the root of salire to leap, spring; cf. F. exil. Cf. Sole of the foot, Saltation.]

senses.d: To banish or expel from one's own country or home; to drive away.
q: Calling home our exiled friends abroad.

senses.d: Small; slender; thin; fine.
One who expels evil spirits by conjuration or exorcism.
q: Certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists.

senses.d: A conjurer who can raise spirits.
q: Thou, like an exorcist, hast conjured up My mortified spirit.

Exorcist.etym: [L. exorcista, Gr. εξορκιστἤσ: cf. F. exorciste.]

senses.d: To wait for; to await.
q: Let's in, and there expect their coming.

senses.d: To look for (mentally); to look forward to, as to something that is believed to be about to happen or come; to have a previous apprehension of, whether of good or evil; to look for with some confidence; to anticipate; — often followed by an infinitive, sometimes by a clause (with, or without, that); as, I expect to receive wages; I expect that the troops will be defeated.
q: The Somersetshire or yellow regiment . . . was expected to arrive on the following day.

Expect.syn: To anticipate; look for; await; hope.
Expect.etym: [L. expectatum, to look out for, await, expect; ex + out spectare to look at. See Spectacle.]

senses.d: To wait; to stay.
Expectation.
The act or state of expecting or looking forward to an event as about to happen.
q: My soul, wait thou only upon God, for my expectation is from him.

senses.d: That which is expected or looked for.
q: Why our great expectation should be called The seed of woman.

senses.d: The prospect of the future; grounds upon which something excellent is expected to happen; prospect of anything good to come, esp. of property or rank.
q: His magnificent expectations made him, in the opinion of the world, the best match in Europe.
By all men's eyes a youth of expectation.

senses.d: The value of any chance (as the prospect of prize or property) which depends upon some contingent event. Expectations are computed for or against the occurrence of the event.
The leaving of the disease principally to the efforts of nature to effect a cure.

Hastening or forward; hence, tending to further or promote a proposed object; fit or proper under the circumstances; conducive to self-interest; desirable; advisable; advantageous; — sometimes contradistinguished from right.
q: It is expedient for you that I go away.
Nothing but the right can ever be expedient, since that can never be true expediency which would sacrifice a greater good to a less.

senses.d: Quick; expeditious.
q: His marches are expedient to this town.

Expedient.etym: [L. expediens, -entis, p. pr. of expedire to be expedient, release, extricate: cf. F. expédient. See Expedite.]

senses.d: That which serves to promote or advance; suitable means to accomplish an end.
q: What sure expedient than shall Juno find, To calm her fears and ease her boding mind?

senses.d: Means devised in an exigency; shift.
To drive or force out from that within which anything is contained, inclosed, or situated; to eject; as, to expel air from a bellows.
q: Did not ye . . . expel me out of my father's house?

senses.d: To drive away from one's country; to banish.
q: Forewasted all their land, and them expelled.
He shall expel them from before you . . . and ye shall possess their land.

senses.d: To cut off from further connection with an institution of learning, a society, and the like; as, to expel a student or member.
To keep out, off, or away; to exclude.
To discharge; to shoot.
q: Then he another and another did expel.

Expel.syn: To banish; exile; eject; drive out. See Banish.
Expel.etym: [L. expellere, expulsum; ex out + pellere to drive: cf.F. expeller. See Pulse a beat.]

senses.d: A spending or consuming; disbursement; expenditure.
q: Husband nature's riches from expense.

senses.d: That which is expended, laid out, or consumed; cost; outlay; charge; — sometimes with the notion of loss or damage to those on whom the expense falls; as, the expenses of war; an expense of time.
q: Courting popularity at his party's expense.

senses.d: Loss.
q: And moan the expense of many a vanished sight.

Expense.etym: [L. expensa (sc. pecunia), or expensum, fr. expensus, p. p. of expendere. See Expend.]

senses.d: Trial, as a test or experiment.
q: She caused him to make experience Upon wild beasts.

senses.d: The effect upon the judgment or feelings produced by any event, whether witnessed or participated in; personal and direct impressions as contrasted with description or fancies; personal acquaintance; actual enjoyment or suffering.
q: I have but one lamp by which my feet are guided, and that is the lamp of experience.
To most men experience is like the stern lights of a ship, which illumine only the track it has passed.
When the consuls . . . came in . . . they knew soon by experience how slenderly guarded against danger the majesty of rulers is where force is wanting.
Those that undertook the religion of our Savior upon his preaching, had no experience of it.

senses.d: An act of knowledge, one or more, by which single facts or general truths are ascertained; experimental or inductive knowledge; hence, implying skill, facility, or practical wisdom gained by personal knowledge, feeling or action; as, a king without experience of war.
q: Whence hath the mind all the materials of reason and knowledge? To this I answer in one word, from experience.

Experience may be acquired in two ways; either, first by noticing facts without any attempt to influence the frequency of their occurrence or to vary the circumstances under which they occur; this is observation; or, secondly, by putting in action causes or agents over which we have control, and purposely varying their combinations, and noticing what effects take place; this is experiment.

Experience.etym: [F. expérience, L. experientia, tr. experiens, experientis, p. pr. of experiri, expertus, to try; ex out + the root of peritus experienced. See Peril, and cf. Expert.]

senses.d: To make practical acquaintance with; to try personally; to prove by use or trial; to have trial of; to have the lot or fortune of; to have befall one; to be affected by; to feel; as, to experience pain or pleasure; to experience poverty; to experience a change of views.
q: The partial failure and disappointment which he had experienced in India.

senses.d: To exercise; to train by practice.
q: The youthful sailors thus with early care Their arms experience, and for sea prepare.

senses.d: A trial or special observation, made to confirm or disprove something doubtful; esp., one under conditions determined by the experimenter; an act or operation undertaken in order to discover some unknown principle or effect, or to test, establish, or illustrate some suggested or known truth; practical test; proof.
q: A political experiment can not be made in a laboratory, nor determined in a few hours.

senses.d: Experience.
q: Adam, by sad experiment I know How little weight my words with thee can find.

Experiment.etym: [L. experimentum, fr. experiri to try: cf. OF. esperiment, experiment. See Experience.]

senses.d: To make experiment; to operate by test or trial; — often with on, upon, or in, referring to the subject of an experiment; with, referring to the instrument; and by, referring to the means; as, to experiment upon electricity; he experimented in plowing with ponies, or by steam power.
To try; to know, perceive, or prove, by trial or experience.

Taught by use, practice, or experience, experienced; having facility of operation or performance from practice; knowing and ready from much practice; clever; skillful; as, an expert surgeon; expert in chess or archery.
q: A valiant and most expert gentleman.
What practice, howsoe'er expert In fitting aptest words to things . . . Hath power to give thee as thou wert?

Expert.etym: [F. expert, L. expertus, p. p. of experiri to try. See Experience.]

senses.d: An expert or experienced person; one instructed by experience; one who has skill, experience, or extensive knowledge in his calling or in any special branch of learning.
A specialist in a particular profession or department of science requiring for its mastery peculiar culture and erudition.
A sworn appraiser.
To experience.
q: Die would we daily, once it to expert.

senses.d: To breathe out; to emit from the lungs; to throw out from the mouth or nostrils in the process of respiration; — opposed to inspire.
q: Anatomy exhibits the lungs in a continual motion of inspiring and expiring air.
This chafed the boar; his nostrils flames expire.

senses.d: To give forth insensibly or gently, as a fluid or vapor; to emit in minute particles; to exhale; as, the earth expires a damp vapor; plants expire odors.
q: The expiring of cold out of the inward parts of the earth in winter.

senses.d: To emit; to give out.
To bring to a close; to terminate.
q: Expire the term Of a despised life.

Expire.etym: [L. expirare, exspirare, expiratum, exspiratum; ex out + spirare to breathe: cf. F. expirer. See Spirit.]

senses.d: To emit the breath.
To emit the last breath; to breathe out the life; to die; as, to expire calmly; to expire in agony.
To come to an end; to cease; to terminate; to perish; to become extinct; as, the flame expired; his lease expires to-day; the month expired on Saturday.
To burst forth; to fly out with a blast.
A deed or act; especially, a heroic act; a deed of renown; an adventurous or noble achievement; as, the exploits of Alexander the Great.
q: Ripe for exploits and mighty enterprises.

senses.d: Combat; war.
q: He made haste to exploit some warlike service.

senses.d: To utilize; to make available; to get the value or usefulness out of; as, to exploit a mine or agricultural lands; to exploit public opinion.
Hence: To draw an illegitimate profit from; to speculate on; to put upon.
q: In no sense whatever does a man who accumulates a fortune by legitimate industry exploit his employés or make his capital “out of” anybody else.

Exploit.etym: [OE. esploit success, OF. esploit, espleit,revenue, product, vigor, force, exploit, F. exploit exploit, fr. L. explicitum, prop. p. p. neut. of explicare to unfold, display, exhibit; ex + plicare to fold. See Ply, and cf. Explicit, Explicate.]

senses.d: To lay open; to expose to view; to examine.
q: He expounded both his pockets.

senses.d: To lay open the meaning of; to explain; to clear of obscurity; to interpret; as, to expound a text of Scripture, a law, a word, a meaning, or a riddle.
q: Expound this matter more fully to me.

Expound.etym: [OE. exponen, expounen, expounden, fr. L. exponere to set out, expose, expound; ex out + ponere to put: cf. OE. expondre, expondre. See Position.]

senses.d: Exactly representing; exact.
q: Their human countenance The express resemblance of the gods.

senses.d: Directly and distinctly stated; declared in terms; not implied or left to inference; made unambiguous by intention and care; clear; not dubious; as, express consent; an express statement.
q: I have express commandment.

senses.d: Intended for a particular purpose; relating to an express; sent on a particular errand; dispatched with special speed; as, an express messenger or train. Also used adverbially.
q: A messenger sent express from the other world.

Express.etym: [F. exprès, L. expressus, p. p. of exprimere to express; ex. out + premere To press. See Press.]

senses.d: A clear image or representation; an expression; a plain declaration.
q: The only remanent express of Christ's sacrifice on earth.

senses.d: A messenger sent on a special errand; a courier; hence, a regular and fast conveyance; commonly, a company or system for the prompt and safe transportation of merchandise or parcels; also, a railway train for transporting passengers or goods with speed and punctuality.
An express office.
q: She charged him . . . to ask at the express if anything came up from town.

senses.d: That which is sent by an express messenger or message.
To press or squeeze out; as, to express the juice of grapes, or of apples; hence, to extort; to elicit.
q: All the fruits out of which drink is expressed.
And th'idle breath all utterly expressed.
Halters and racks can not express from thee More than by deeds.

senses.d: To make or offer a representation of; to show by a copy or likeness; to represent; to resemble.
q: Each skillful artist shall express thy form.
So kids and whelps their sires and dams express.

senses.d: To give a true impression of; to represent and make known; to manifest plainly; to show in general; to exhibit, as an opinion or feeling, by a look, gesture, and esp. by language; to declare; to utter; to tell.
q: My words express my purpose.
They expressed in their lives those excellent doctrines of morality.

senses.d: To make known the opinions or feelings of; to declare what is in the mind of; to show (one's self); to cause to appear; — used reflexively.
q: Mr. Phillips did express with much indignation against me, one evening.

senses.d: To denote; to designate.
q: Moses and Aaron took these men, which are expressed by their names.

senses.d: To send by express messenger; to forward by special opportunity, or through the medium of an express; as, to express a package.

Express.syn: To declare; utter; signify; testify; intimate.
Express.etym: [Cf. OF. espresser, expresser, L. exprimere, expressum. See Express, a.; cf. Sprain.]

senses.d: In an express manner; in direct terms; with distinct purpose; particularly; as, a book written expressly for the young.
q: The word of the Lord came expressly unto Ezekiel.
I am sent expressly to your lordship.

senses.d: To stretch out; to prolong in space; to carry forward or continue in length; as, to extend a line in surveying; to extend a cord across the street.
q: Few extend their thoughts toward universal knowledge.

senses.d: To enlarge, as a surface or volume; to expand; to spread; to amplify; as, to extend metal plates by hammering or rolling them.

To enlarge; to widen; to carry out further; as, to extend the capacities, the sphere of usefulness, or commerce; to extend power or influence; to continue, as time; to lengthen; to prolong; as, to extend the time of payment or a season of trial.
To hold out or reach forth, as the arm or hand.
q: His helpless hand extend.

senses.d: To bestow; to offer; to impart; to apply; as, to extend sympathy to the suffering.
To increase in quantity by weakening or adulterating additions; as, to extend liquors.
To value, as lands taken by a writ of extent in satisfaction of a debt; to assign by writ of extent.

Extend.syn: To increase; enlarge; expand; widen; diffuse. See Increase.
Extend.etym: [L. extendere, extentum, extensum; ex out + tendere to stretch. See Trend.]

senses.d: Extinguished; put out; quenched; as, a fire, a light, or a lamp, is extinct; an extinct volcano.
q: Light, the prime work of God, to me is extinct.

senses.d: Without a survivor; without force; dead; as, a family becomes extinct; an extinct feud or law.

Extinct.etym: [L. extinctus, exstinctus, p. p. of extinguere, exstinguere. See Extinguish.]

senses.d: To cause to be extinct.
To place on high; to lift up; to elevate.
q: Who extolled you in the half-crown boxes, Where you might sit and muster all the beauties.

senses.d: To elevate by praise; to eulogize; to praise; to magnify; as, to extol virtue; to extol an act or a person.
